blocks.html: In Civics you met the rule of law: no one is above the law, and the law is known in advance. This course asks the next questions. What is a law? Where does it come from? How do lawyers and judges reason with it? We start with the first question, because the answer shapes everything after it.

Law is the set of rules that a government makes or recognizes and that courts and officials enforce. It overlaps with morality (what is right and wrong) and custom (what people usually do), but it differs from both in who makes it and how it is enforced.

Morality
Custom and manners

blocks.html: Why have law at all, when most people already follow their consciences? Because people disagree about what is right, and some disputes must be settled one way or the other. Law gives a public, settled answer that applies to everyone, made by a known process and backed by the power of the state. It lets strangers plan (a contract will be enforced), protects people from harm (assault is punished), and coordinates choices that could go either way (everyone drives on the right). Morality cannot do those jobs alone, because it has no single author and no courthouse.

blocks.text: Law and morality: two classic views

blocks.html: Philosophers have long debated how law and morality connect. In the natural law tradition (Cicero, Thomas Aquinas, and the "Laws of Nature" in the Declaration of Independence), human law takes its authority partly from a higher standard of justice, so a gravely unjust rule is a defective law. Legal positivists (John Austin, H. L. A. Hart) answer that a rule is law because of its source: it was made by the recognized process. Whether it is just is a separate and important question. Hart and Lon Fuller debated these views in the Harvard Law Review in 1958, and the debate continues. Both sides agree that law and morality differ and that both matter; they disagree about how to describe the line between them.

blocks.title: Legal, and right?
blocks.q: Sort each act two ways, as legal or illegal and as widely thought right or wrong: (a) breaking a casual promise to help a friend move; (b) driving 40 mph in a 35 mph zone on an empty road at dawn; (c) before 1865, helping a person escape slavery.
steps: (a) Breaking a casual promise is usually legal: a social promise is not a contract. Many people think it is wrong.
(b) It is illegal: the speed limit is a rule. Many people see little moral wrong in it, but the law still applies.
(c) The Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 made it a federal crime, so it was illegal. Today it is almost universally seen as right.
So "legal" and "right" can come apart in both directions. Law is identified by its sources and enforcement, not by whether we approve.
blocks.a: (a) legal, often thought wrong; (b) illegal, often thought minor; (c) illegal then, widely thought right.

Some lawful acts are widely thought wrong (breaking a casual promise), and some unlawful acts were once widely thought right (helping people escape slavery). When you ask "is it legal?", look for a source (a constitution, statute, regulation or case) and an enforcer. When you ask "is it right?", you are asking a moral question, which the law may or may not answer the same way.

blocks.html: When a lawyer is asked a question, the first job is to find the law that answers it. American law does not live in one book. It comes from several sources, made by different bodies, and they rank in an order of authority. This lesson builds on what law is.

blocks.html: American law comes from constitutions, statutes, treaties, regulations, court decisions and ordinances. They rank in an order: the U.S. Constitution is highest, then valid federal statutes and treaties, then federal regulations; within a state, its constitution outranks its statutes, which outrank its regulations and local ordinances.

Why an order? Because each lower source gets its authority from a higher one. An agency may write a regulation only because a statute gave it that power, so a regulation that goes beyond the statute is invalid. A legislature may pass statutes only within the limits of its constitution, so an unconstitutional statute is void. Follow the chain upward and you reach the people, who adopted the constitutions. Courts sit beside this ladder: they decide cases under every source and, where no statute speaks, they apply the common law they have built case by case.

blocks.title: A regulation that goes too far
blocks.q: A statute lets an agency set safety rules for "commercial trucks." The agency issues a rule for private pickup trucks used only for family errands. Is the rule valid?
steps: Find the source of the agency's power: the statute.
The statute reaches commercial trucks. Family pickups are not commercial.
A regulation cannot go beyond the authority the statute delegates.
blocks.a: No. The rule exceeds the statute, so a court would set it aside.

blocks.title: A city against its state
blocks.q: A state statute sets the speed limit on all state highways at 65 mph. A town passes an ordinance setting 55 mph on the state highway that runs through it, and the statute does not allow towns to change it. Which rule controls?
steps: Ordinances rank below state statutes. Cities and counties have only the powers their state gives them.
The two rules conflict on the same road.
Unless state law lets the town set its own limit, the state statute controls.
blocks.a: The state statute (65 mph).

blocks.html: Lawyers also separate primary authority (the law itself: the sources above) from secondary authority (writing about the law: treatises, law review articles, the Restatements). Secondary sources can explain and persuade, but they are not law.

Thinking only legislatures make law. Agencies write binding regulations (the Federal Register, where they are published, runs to tens of thousands of pages a year), courts make the common law and interpret every other source, and the people make constitutions. A quick check: ask "who made this rule, and where did they get the power to make it?"
This is an educational course, not legal advice.

The United States has two layers of government, as you saw in federalism. So every place in the country has two bodies of law at once: federal law and the law of its state. Most of the time they fit together. When they clash, the Constitution says which one wins, and how far that win reaches.

blocks.html: Under the Supremacy Clause, a valid federal law overrides a conflicting state law. This is called preemption. Where there is no valid federal law or no conflict, state law governs, and states make most of the law people meet day to day.

items: Express preemption: Congress says in the statute that state laws on the subject are displaced.
Field preemption: federal regulation is so complete that Congress left no room for the states in that field.
Conflict preemption: it is impossible to obey both laws, or the state law stands as an obstacle to the federal law's purposes.

blocks.html: The national government has only the powers the Constitution lists; the rest are reserved to the states (the Tenth Amendment). So supremacy has two built-in limits. First, a federal law must be valid: within Congress's powers and consistent with the Constitution. Second, there must be conflict or displacement. That is why criminal law, family law, property, contracts and torts are mostly state law, and why each state has its own constitution, statutes and courts. Each state's highest court has the last word on what its own state law means.

blocks.title: Two minimum wages
blocks.q: The federal minimum wage is \$7.25 an hour. A state sets its minimum at \$15. An employer says federal law preempts the state law. Is the employer right?
steps: Is there a conflict? An employer can obey both by paying \$15, which is above \$7.25.
The federal law sets a floor and does not say states may not go higher.
No conflict and no displacement, so both apply.
blocks.a: No. The employer must pay the state's \$15.

blocks.title: Impossible to obey both
blocks.q: A federal statute requires a warning label in exact federal wording and forbids changes. A state law requires a different warning on the same label. What happens?
steps: A maker cannot follow both: the federal law forbids the change the state requires.
That is conflict preemption (and the statute may preempt expressly too).
If the federal law is valid, the state requirement gives way.
blocks.a: The state requirement is preempted.

blocks.html: The same act can break both laws. Because the states and the nation are separate sovereigns, each may prosecute it under its own law without violating double jeopardy: the Supreme Court reaffirmed this "dual sovereignty" rule in Gamble v. United States (2019). And a state constitution can protect rights more broadly than the federal Constitution, as long as it does not take away federal rights.

If the answer to (2) is "yes, both can be obeyed, and no displacement," both laws apply.

blocks.html: Law schools and courts divide the law into fields. One of the oldest divisions, going back to Roman law, is between public law and private law. It helps you guess who the parties will be and what kind of rules apply. It builds on the sources of law.

Public law governs the relation between the government and people: constitutional, administrative and criminal law. Private law governs relations among people and organizations: contracts, torts, property, family law and business law.

What it covers

What it covers

blocks.html: The line follows whose interest is at stake and who may bring the case. In public law, the government acts as the government: it prosecutes, regulates or taxes, and it is limited by the Constitution. In private law, the government acts as a referee: its courts settle disputes between private parties, and the injured party decides whether to sue. That is why a crime is prosecuted by "the State" or "the People" even though one person was harmed: the law treats a crime as a wrong against the whole community.

blocks.title: One event, two fields
blocks.q: Dana shoves Lee in a parking lot and breaks Lee's glasses. Which body of law applies?
steps: Criminal law (public): the state may charge Dana with assault or battery. The prosecutor decides, not Lee.
Tort law (private): Lee may sue Dana for battery to get money for the glasses and any injury.
The two cases are separate, with different parties and different rules.
blocks.a: Both: a public criminal case (State v. Dana) and a private tort suit (Lee v. Dana).

blocks.title: The government as a private party
blocks.q: A city signs a contract to buy fire trucks and then refuses to pay. Public or private law?
steps: The dispute is over a contract, a private-law subject.
The city is acting much like any buyer, so contract law mostly governs, though special rules may apply to suits against governments.
blocks.a: Mainly private law (contracts), even though a government is a party.

blocks.html: Placing criminal law in private law because a person was harmed. A crime is an offense against the public, prosecuted by the government; the victim does not control the case and cannot drop the charges. The victim's own claim for money is a separate, private case. Check: who is the party bringing the case? If it is the government enforcing a criminal law, it is public law.
This is an educational course, not legal advice.

The most practical split in American law is between civil and criminal cases. They use different courtrooms, rules and standards of proof, and they end in different results. You saw the roots of the split in public and private law.

blocks.html: In a criminal case the government prosecutes and must prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. In a civil case a plaintiff sues for a remedy and usually must prove the claim by a preponderance of the evidence. One act can lead to both kinds of case.

Why is the criminal standard so much higher? A conviction can take away liberty and brands a person as a wrongdoer, so the law accepts that some guilty people will go free rather than risk convicting the innocent. The Supreme Court held in In re Winship (1970) that due process requires proof beyond a reasonable doubt of every element of a crime. A civil case is a contest between two parties with equal stakes in getting it right, so the tie-breaker is simply which side's account is more likely true.

blocks.cap: Most civil and criminal cases begin in the same state trial courts, often in different divisions, and follow the same path on appeal.

blocks.title: Acquitted, then sued
blocks.q: A jury finds Sam not guilty of assaulting Rita. Rita then sues Sam for battery. Sam says double jeopardy bars the suit. Is he right?
steps: Double jeopardy bars a second criminal prosecution for the same offense. A civil suit is not a prosecution.
The parties differ: the state then, Rita now.
The standards differ: the jury found guilt not proven beyond a reasonable doubt. That leaves room for a finding that battery is more likely than not.
blocks.a: No. The civil suit may go forward, and Rita can win under the lower standard.

blocks.title: Name the case
blocks.q: A company dumps waste into a river. (1) The state charges the company under its environmental crimes law. (2) A farmer downstream sues for damage to her crops. Civil or criminal?
steps: (1) The government prosecutes for a crime: criminal. It must prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt; the penalty is a fine.
(2) A private party seeks money for harm: civil. Preponderance of the evidence.
blocks.a: (1) criminal; (2) civil.

blocks.html: Thinking a not-guilty verdict prevents a civil suit for the same act. An acquittal means only that guilt was not proven beyond a reasonable doubt. Double jeopardy applies only to criminal prosecutions, and the civil case has a different plaintiff and a lower standard. Check: is the second case a prosecution by the government? If not, double jeopardy does not apply.

One of the sources of law is unusual: law made by judges, one case at a time. That is the common law, and it is the reason American lawyers spend so much time reading old cases.

The common law grew from the decisions of English royal judges, case by case, and the United States inherited it. Civil law systems, in much of Europe and Latin America, start instead from comprehensive written codes. Louisiana's private law draws on the civil law tradition.

events.label: Henry II becomes king; royal judges ride circuits

blocks.cap: Two traditions, one built from cases and one from codes.

blocks.html: In the 1100s, King Henry II sent royal judges around England to hear disputes. They decided cases by the customs and earlier decisions of the king's courts, and because the same judges met and compared notes, a law common to the whole kingdom grew up. Each decision became a reason for deciding the next like case the same way. William Blackstone's Commentaries on the Laws of England (1765–1769) organized that law into a system, and American lawyers learned from it. After independence, most states passed reception statutes adopting English common law as of a set date, so far as it fit American conditions. Louisiana, shaped by French and Spanish rule before the 1803 purchase, built its private law on a civil code instead.

Civil law tradition
rows: influential, but formally the code governs
often shorter, focused on the code's articles
England, the United States (except Louisiana private law), Canada (except Quebec), Australia, India
France, Germany, Spain, most of Latin America, Japan, Quebec

blocks.title: Where does the rule come from?
blocks.q: A court must decide whether a store owner owes a duty of care to a customer who slipped on a wet floor. No statute addresses it. Where does the court look?
steps: No statute or regulation speaks, so the court looks to the common law of torts.
It reads earlier decisions of its own state's courts on store owners and customers.
It applies the rule those cases set, adjusting for any new facts.
blocks.a: To precedent: the state's common law of negligence, built from earlier cases.

blocks.title: When a statute speaks
blocks.q: Later, the state legislature passes a statute on store owners' duties. Does the common law still control?
steps: Statutes outrank judge-made common law.
Where the statute speaks, it controls; where it is silent, the common law fills the gaps.
Courts still interpret the statute, and their readings become precedent too.
blocks.a: No: the statute controls where it applies; the common law fills the gaps.

blocks.html: Thinking civil law systems ignore past cases and common law systems ignore statutes. Both use codes and cases. Much American law is now in statutes (criminal codes, the Uniform Commercial Code), and judges in civil law countries do read and follow earlier decisions. The difference is emphasis and the formal weight given to precedent. And do not confuse the civil law tradition (codes) with civil cases (non-criminal suits): same word, different meaning.
This is an educational course, not legal advice.
The common law works only if courts treat past decisions as rules for the future. The doctrine that makes them do so has a Latin name.

Stare decisis ("to stand by things decided") means courts follow precedent. Vertical stare decisis: lower courts must follow the decisions of higher courts in their system. Horizontal stare decisis: a court usually follows its own earlier decisions, but it may overrule them for strong reasons.

blocks.name: cv-court
blocks.cap: Vertical stare decisis: a federal court of appeals binds the district courts below it (in its own circuit).

blocks.html: Why follow precedent even when a judge thinks it is wrong? Four reasons are usually given. Predictability: people can plan when they know how courts will rule. Equal treatment: like cases are decided alike, whoever the judge is. Efficiency: courts need not reargue every question in every case. Legitimacy and restraint: the law looks less like the preference of whoever is on the bench. The cost is that an error can last. So the vertical rule is strict (a trial judge may not ignore the state supreme court), while the horizontal rule is a strong presumption, not an absolute command.

head: Vertical
Horizontal
rows: lower courts in the same system
the same court (and, in many systems, other panels of it)
mandatory: a lower court may not overrule a higher court
a strong presumption; the court may overrule itself
a federal district court in Ohio follows the Sixth Circuit and the Supreme Court
the Supreme Court follows its own past rulings unless it decides to overrule one

blocks.title: A trial judge who disagrees
blocks.q: A state trial judge thinks a ruling of her state's supreme court is badly reasoned. May she decide the case the other way?
steps: This is vertical stare decisis: the state supreme court is above her in the same system.
She must follow it. She may write that she disagrees and explain why, which may help the higher court reconsider.
Only the state supreme court (or the legislature, for a statutory ruling) can change the rule.
blocks.a: No. She must follow the higher court's precedent.

blocks.title: A high court changes its mind
blocks.q: In 1940 the Supreme Court upheld a public school's required flag salute (Minersville School District v. Gobitis). In 1943 it struck down such a requirement in West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette. How could it?
steps: Horizontal stare decisis is a presumption, not an absolute rule.
In Barnette the Court concluded Gobitis was wrongly reasoned and overruled it.
From then on, lower courts were bound by Barnette.
blocks.a: The Court overruled its own precedent, which horizontal stare decisis allows for strong reasons.

blocks.html: Judges and scholars disagree about how much weight precedent deserves. Some stress that stability and reliance are themselves important values, especially when people have built their lives and businesses around a rule. Others argue that a precedent clearly wrong about the Constitution deserves less weight, because the Constitution, not the earlier decision, is the supreme law. The Court has also said precedents interpreting statutes deserve extra respect, since Congress can change a statute if it disagrees with the Court's reading.

Thinking a court may never depart from its own precedent. Vertical stare decisis is strict, but horizontal stare decisis can be overcome, and the Supreme Court has overruled itself many times (for example, Brown v. Board of Education rejected Plessy's "separate but equal" for public schools). Check: is the precedent from a higher court (must follow) or the same court (presumption, may overrule)?
This is an educational course, not legal advice.

blocks.html: Stare decisis tells a court to follow precedent, but not every precedent. Before a lawyer cites a case, she asks: does this decision bind the court I am in, or can it only persuade?

A decision is binding (mandatory) authority on the courts below it in the same system, and on the same court. Decisions from other states, other federal circuits or lower courts are only persuasive, and so are secondary sources such as treatises, the Restatements and law review articles.

blocks.name: cv-map
blocks.cap: The federal courts of appeals. A Ninth Circuit ruling binds federal district courts in the Ninth Circuit's states, not those in Texas (Fifth Circuit).

items: U.S. Supreme Court on federal law: binds every court in the country, federal and state.
Federal court of appeals: binds the district courts in its own circuit (and later panels of the same circuit).
State supreme court on its state's law: binds every court of that state, and federal courts applying that state's law.
Persuasive only: other circuits, other states' courts, trial court opinions, dicta, foreign courts, treatises and articles.

blocks.html: Authority follows the chain of review. A court is bound by the courts that can reverse it, because ignoring them would only lead to reversal and unequal treatment. A court in Texas cannot be reversed by a court in California, so California's rulings can only persuade. On questions of a state's own law, the state's highest court has the last word, so a federal court deciding a case under that law (for example, in a diversity case, under Erie Railroad Co. v. Tompkins, 1938) follows the state court's rulings. Persuasive authority still matters: when no binding case answers a question, a well-reasoned opinion from elsewhere can carry the day.

blocks.title: A circuit split
blocks.q: The Fourth Circuit reads a federal statute one way; the Seventh Circuit reads it the other way. A case under the statute is filed in federal district court in Illinois (Seventh Circuit). Which reading binds the court?
steps: Illinois is in the Seventh Circuit, so Seventh Circuit decisions bind the district court there.
The Fourth Circuit's decision is persuasive only.
Disagreement among circuits is a "circuit split," one of the main reasons the Supreme Court grants review: its ruling then binds all of them.
blocks.a: The Seventh Circuit's reading.

blocks.title: Out-of-state precedent
blocks.q: An Oregon trial court faces a new question of Oregon contract law. No Oregon case decides it, but the Supreme Court of California has decided the same question. Must the Oregon court follow it?
steps: California's courts are not above Oregon's; it is a different system.
So the California ruling is persuasive: the Oregon court may adopt its reasoning if it finds it convincing, or reject it.
blocks.a: No. It is persuasive, not binding.

blocks.cap: Supreme Court dicta are not binding, though lower courts give them great weight.

blocks.html: Thinking a federal court of appeals ruling binds every federal court. It binds courts within its own circuit; other circuits may disagree, creating a split that the Supreme Court may resolve. Check: draw the line of appeal. Could the court that decided the precedent reverse the court you are in? If not, the precedent is persuasive.
This is an educational course, not legal advice.
When a precedent is binding, not every sentence in it binds. Judges write a great deal: background, history, asides, predictions. Only part of an opinion is the rule later courts must follow.

The holding is the rule of law necessary to decide the case on its facts. Dicta (singular: dictum; from obiter dictum, "something said in passing") are statements that were not necessary to the decision. Holdings bind later courts; dicta can only persuade.

Why should only the holding bind? A court decides the dispute in front of it, after hearing both sides argue the questions that matter to that dispute. Remarks about other situations were not tested by argument and were not needed for the result, so treating them as law would let a court decide cases that were never before it. A classic way to tell the difference is Wambaugh's inversion test: reverse the statement and ask whether the outcome would change. If removing or reversing a proposition would not change the result, it is probably dictum.

blocks.name: cv-case

opts.name: Rivera v. Harbor Marina (an invented case)
opts.facts: Rivera slipped on an oily dock at a marina where she had paid to keep her boat. The trial court dismissed her negligence claim, ruling that the marina owed her no duty.
opts.q: Does a marina owe a duty of reasonable care to paying customers on its docks?
opts.reasoning: A business that invites paying customers onto its property must use reasonable care to keep it safe. (The court adds:) "We would likely reach the same result for a trespasser who entered at night."

blocks.cap: An invented case. The holding concerns paying customers; the sentence about trespassers is dictum.

blocks.title: Find the holding
blocks.q: In the Rivera case, which statement is the holding, and which is dictum: (1) a marina owes paying customers a duty of reasonable care on its docks; (2) the same result would likely follow for a night-time trespasser?
steps: Rivera was a paying customer. Statement (1) decides her case: without it, the court could not reverse.
Statement (2) is about a trespasser, a person not before the court. Reverse it ("a trespasser would lose") and Rivera still wins.
So (2) was not necessary to the result.
blocks.a: (1) is the holding; (2) is dictum.

blocks.title: A famous footnote
blocks.q: In United States v. Carolene Products Co. (1938) the Court upheld a federal ban on "filled milk" under a deferential test. Footnote four suggested that courts might look harder at laws aimed at "discrete and insular minorities." Holding or dictum?
steps: The case was decided under the deferential test: the ban was upheld.
The footnote speculated about other kinds of laws not before the Court, so it was not needed to decide the case.
It was dictum. Yet it became one of the most influential passages in constitutional law, shaping later doctrine.
blocks.a: Dictum, though later courts built on it.

blocks.html: The line is not always sharp. Later courts often decide how broadly to read a holding: as a narrow rule tied to the precise facts, or a wider principle. Lawyers on each side will argue for the reading that helps their client. And lower courts usually give great weight to considered dicta from the Supreme Court, even though they are not strictly bound.

Treating every sentence in an opinion as law. Ask: if this statement were removed or reversed, would the result change? If not, it is probably dictum. Check the facts too: a statement about parties or situations not before the court (other plaintiffs, other statutes, "even if…") is a warning sign.
This is an educational course, not legal advice.

Suppose a precedent seems to cut against your client. A lawyer has two main moves: show that the precedent does not reach these facts, or, in the court that made it, argue that it should be abandoned. Both depend on knowing the holding.

To distinguish a precedent is to show that the material facts differ, so its holding does not apply; the precedent stays good law. To overrule a precedent is to end its authority; only the court that made it, or a higher court, can do so.

Distinguishing is the everyday tool of the common law. Each case decides only what its facts present, so a new case with a different material fact may need a different answer. Overruling is rarer and more serious. Under stare decisis the Supreme Court asks whether there is a special justification to overrule. In recent cases, such as Janus v. AFSCME (2018), it has named factors including: the quality of the earlier reasoning; the workability of the rule it set; its consistency with related decisions; developments since it was decided (in law or in the understanding of facts); and reliance on it.

blocks.title: Distinguishing
blocks.q: A precedent held a landlord liable when a tenant was hurt by a broken stair the landlord had been told about. Now a tenant is hurt by a stair that broke an hour before the fall, with no notice to the landlord. How might the landlord distinguish the precedent?
steps: Find the facts the earlier court relied on: the landlord knew about the broken stair and did nothing.
Here the landlord had no notice and no time to fix it.
Argue that notice was a material fact, so the earlier holding does not reach this case. The precedent is not wrong; it is different.
blocks.a: By showing a material fact (notice) differs.

blocks.title: Other ways a precedent ends
blocks.q: In Ledbetter v. Goodyear (2007) the Court read a deadline in an employment discrimination statute narrowly. In 2009 Congress passed the Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act. What happened to the precedent?
steps: Ledbetter interpreted a statute, so Congress could change the statute.
The new act changed the rule for when the deadline runs, displacing the Court's reading.

Constitutional decisions can be changed this way only by amendment: the Eleventh Amendment (1795) answered Chisholm v. Georgia (1793), and the Twenty-sixth (1971) answered part of Oregon v. Mitchell (1970).
blocks.a: Congress superseded it by statute.

blocks.html: Thinking distinguishing a case means it was wrongly decided. Distinguishing leaves the precedent intact and says only that it does not reach these facts; overruling ends its authority. Another common slip: thinking a lower court can overrule a higher court's precedent. It can distinguish it, but only the higher court (or the legislature, for statutes) can undo it.

blocks.html: In Civics you met the federal courts as one branch of government. Now we look at them as a lawyer does: which court hears what, which judges hold which offices, and how a case climbs from one level to the next.

blocks.name: cv-court
blocks.cap: The three levels of the federal courts and the usual path of an appeal.

blocks.html: The Article III courts are 94 district courts (trial courts), 13 courts of appeals (12 regional circuits plus the Federal Circuit) and the Supreme Court. Their judges serve "during good Behaviour," which means for life unless removed by impeachment, and their pay cannot be cut. Congress has also created judges without life tenure, such as bankruptcy judges and magistrate judges.

head: Court
Number
What it does
rows: 94: 89 in the states, plus D.C., Puerto Rico, Guam, the Virgin Islands and the Northern Mariana Islands
trial courts: witnesses, evidence, juries; at least one in every state
13: the First through Eleventh Circuits, the D.C. Circuit and the Federal Circuit
hear appeals from district courts and some agencies, usually in panels of three judges
hears appeals it chooses by writ of certiorari, plus a few cases in its original jurisdiction, such as suits between states
for example the Court of International Trade and the Court of Federal Claims
trade cases; money claims against the United States

blocks.html: Article III gives the judicial power to "one supreme Court" and to lower courts that Congress chooses to create. The Constitution protects the judges' independence with tenure during good behavior and protected pay, so they can rule against the President or Congress without fear for their jobs. Congress built the lower courts in layers so that every party gets one appeal as of right (to a court of appeals), while the Supreme Court can choose the cases that matter most for national law. It reviews only a small share of the thousands of petitions it receives each year; by custom, four of the nine justices must vote to grant review (the rule of four).

blocks.title: Trace an appeal
blocks.q: A company loses a patent case in the federal district court in Delaware. Where does it appeal, and then where?
steps: Most appeals go to the regional circuit (for Delaware, the Third Circuit).
But patent appeals go to the Federal Circuit, which hears certain subjects nationwide.
After that, the loser may petition the Supreme Court for certiorari, which it may grant or deny.
blocks.a: To the Federal Circuit, then a petition for certiorari to the Supreme Court.

blocks.title: From a state court
blocks.q: The highest court of Ohio decides a case under Ohio contract law. Can the losing party appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court?
steps: The U.S. Supreme Court may review state court decisions only on questions of federal law (the Constitution, federal statutes, treaties). It confirmed this power in Martin v. Hunter's Lessee (1816).
A pure question of Ohio law has no federal question in it.
The Ohio Supreme Court has the last word on Ohio law.
blocks.a: No, unless the case also raises a federal question.

blocks.html: Thinking federal courts are "higher" than state courts in every matter. They are separate systems. A state supreme court is the final authority on its state's law, and federal district courts do not review state courts. The only link at the top is the U.S. Supreme Court, and only on federal questions. Check: is the question about federal law? If not, the state's highest court is the end of the line.
This is an educational course, not legal advice.

sources.name: Grokipedia, "Federal judiciary of the United States"

blocks.html: Most Americans who ever go to court go to a state court: for a traffic ticket, a divorce, a will, a landlord dispute or a criminal charge. Each state builds its own system, so names and details vary, but the shape is much like the federal courts.

blocks.name: cv-court
blocks.cap: Two parallel systems. State courts hear the great majority of the country's cases.

blocks.html: Most states have trial courts (often both limited-jurisdiction courts, such as traffic, small claims and probate, and general-jurisdiction courts), an intermediate appellate court, and a highest court, usually called the supreme court. Each state's highest court has the final word on that state's law.

head: State
Trial court of general jurisdiction
Highest court
rows: often called the circuit, district or superior court
two: the Supreme Court (civil) and the Court of Criminal Appeals (criminal)
blocks.cap: Names vary. Identify a court by its place in the system, not its title.

blocks.html: The Constitution created a federal government of limited powers and left the states with their own governments and courts. Since most law (crimes, contracts, property, family, accidents) is state law, most cases are state cases: by one common estimate, about 95 percent of the nation's civil and criminal cases. State courts also hear many cases involving federal law, because state judges are bound by the Supremacy Clause and usually share jurisdiction with federal courts. States choose judges in different ways: partisan or nonpartisan elections, appointment by the governor, or "merit selection" with later retention elections.

blocks.title: Read the court's name
blocks.q: A news story says "the New York Supreme Court ruled today." Has New York's highest court decided the case?
steps: In New York, the Supreme Court is the main trial court.
Appeals go to its Appellate Division and then to the Court of Appeals, the highest court.
So the story describes a trial-level ruling, which may be appealed.
blocks.a: No. It was a trial court ruling.

blocks.title: Which court is last?
blocks.q: A defendant is convicted of a crime in a Texas district court and loses in the intermediate court of appeals. Which Texas court is the last stop on Texas law?
steps: Texas splits its top level: civil cases go to the Supreme Court of Texas, criminal cases to the Court of Criminal Appeals.
This is a criminal case.
blocks.a: The Texas Court of Criminal Appeals.

cards.text: A speeding ticket
A divorce

Probate of a will
A bankruptcy petition
A dispute over a used-car sale

blocks.html: Assuming every state's "Supreme Court" is its highest court. In New York it is a trial court, and Texas and Oklahoma have two highest courts. Check the court's place in the system: does any other court of the state review its decisions? If so, it is not the highest.
This is an educational course, not legal advice.

Before a court can decide who wins, it must have the power to hear the case at all. That power is jurisdiction. A court needs two kinds: power over the kind of case, and power over the defendant. This builds on state courts and the federal courts.

Subject-matter jurisdiction: federal courts hear only listed kinds of cases, chiefly federal-question cases (arising under federal law) and diversity cases between citizens of different states where more than \$75,000 is at stake. Personal jurisdiction: the defendant must have enough contacts with the state that a suit there is fair.

head: Federal subject-matter jurisdiction
Requirements
rows: the claim arises under the Constitution, a federal statute or a treaty
complete diversity (no plaintiff is a citizen of the same state as any defendant) and an amount in controversy that exceeds \$75,000, not counting interest and costs

blocks.html:
State trial courts of general jurisdiction can hear almost any case. Federal courts are courts of limited jurisdiction: Article III lists the kinds of cases they may hear, and Congress decides how much of that list to give them. Diversity jurisdiction exists so that an out-of-state party need not fear a home-town court. The Supreme Court read the statute to require complete diversity in Strawbridge v. Curtiss (1806). If a case could have been filed in federal court but was filed in state court, the defendant may usually remove it to federal court.

Personal jurisdiction protects defendants under the Due Process Clause. In International Shoe Co. v. Washington (1945) the Court held that a state may hear a suit against an out-of-state defendant with "certain minimum contacts" with the state, so that the suit does not offend "traditional notions of fair play and substantial justice" (326 U.S. at 316). A defendant can always be sued where it is "at home": an individual's home state, or a corporation's state of incorporation and principal place of business.

blocks.title: Complete diversity
blocks.q: Ana (Ohio) and Ben (Michigan) sue Carla (Indiana) and DeShawn (Michigan) in federal court for \$200,000 under state contract law. Is there diversity jurisdiction?
steps: No federal law is involved, so diversity is the only route.
Amount: \$200,000 exceeds \$75,000. That part is met.
Citizenship: plaintiff Ben and defendant DeShawn are both from Michigan.
Complete diversity fails if any plaintiff shares a state with any defendant.
blocks.a: No. Ben and DeShawn are both Michigan citizens.

blocks.title: A corporation's citizenship
blocks.q: Pat (Texas) sues Acme Inc., incorporated in Delaware with its headquarters in Texas, for \$90,000. Diversity?
steps: A corporation is a citizen of its state of incorporation and the state of its principal place of business.
Acme is a citizen of Delaware and Texas.
Pat is from Texas, so a plaintiff and a defendant share a state.
blocks.a: No diversity. The case belongs in state court unless a federal question appears.

blocks.title: Exactly \$75,000
blocks.q: A New Jersey citizen sues a Florida citizen for exactly \$75,000. Diversity?
steps: The parties are diverse.
The amount must exceed \$75,000. Exactly \$75,000 does not.
blocks.a: No. The claim must be more than \$75,000.

blocks.html: Thinking diversity jurisdiction needs only one plaintiff and one defendant from different states. It requires complete diversity: no plaintiff may share citizenship with any defendant. Check by listing every party's state (two for a corporation) and looking for any match across the "v."
This is an educational course, not legal advice.

blocks.html: Both systems, federal and state, divide their work between trial courts and appellate courts. They do different jobs, and knowing the difference tells you what an appeal can and cannot do.

Trial courts find the facts and apply the law, with witnesses, evidence and often a jury. Appellate courts review the written record for legal error. They review questions of law de novo (fresh, with no deference), findings of fact for clear error, and many trial rulings for abuse of discretion.

head: Standard of review
Used for
How much deference
rows: questions of law: what a statute means, what the elements of a claim are
none: the appellate court decides for itself
facts found by a judge without a jury
a lot: reversed only if the court is left firmly convinced a mistake was made
judgment calls: admitting evidence, managing the trial, many motions
a lot: reversed only if the ruling was unreasonable
the most: upheld if a reasonable jury could have reached them

blocks.html: The split follows each court's strengths. A trial judge and jury see the witnesses, hear their voices and watch them under cross-examination; an appellate court sees only a transcript. So appellate courts defer on facts. But on the law, one court should not be bound by another's view of what a statute means, and uniform answers matter, so appellate courts decide legal questions fresh. Appeals also usually require that an error was preserved by an objection at trial, and an error that did not affect the outcome is harmless and is no reason to reverse.

The judge's finding, after a bench trial, that the light was red
The judge's decision to let a witness testify late
Whether a statute requires intent
The judge's finding that a signature was forged

blocks.title: A new witness on appeal
blocks.q: After losing at trial, Jordan finds a new witness and asks the court of appeals to hear her. What happens?
steps: Appellate courts decide on the record made in the trial court.
They do not take new testimony.
Jordan's path, if any, is a motion in the trial court for a new trial based on newly discovered evidence, which has strict limits.
blocks.a: The appellate court will not hear the witness.

blocks.title: Law or fact?
blocks.q: The trial judge ruled that a statute's word "vehicle" includes bicycles, and then found that Kai rode a bicycle through the park. Kai appeals both points. Which standard applies to each?
steps: The meaning of "vehicle" is a question of law: de novo.
Whether Kai rode a bicycle is a question of fact found by the judge: clear error.
blocks.a: De novo for the meaning of the statute; clear error for what Kai did.

blocks.name: cv-court
blocks.cap: Every federal litigant gets one appeal as of right, to a court of appeals.

blocks.html: Thinking an appeal is a new trial. Appellate courts usually take no new evidence and do not rehear witnesses. They decide whether the trial court made a legal error that affected the result. Check: is the complaint "they got the facts wrong" (a hard argument under clear error or the jury standard) or "they applied the wrong rule" (reviewed fresh)?
This is an educational course, not legal advice.

A civil lawsuit follows a set path. Knowing the stages helps you read any case, because every appellate opinion says at which stage the case left the trial court and that tells you what was decided. Recall the difference between civil and criminal cases.

blocks.name: cv-order
blocks.cap: Put the stages of a civil case in order, then press Check.

blocks.html: A civil case moves from complaint and answer through motions to dismiss, discovery and summary judgment to trial, verdict, judgment and appeal. Most cases never reach trial: they settle, are dismissed, or are decided on motions.

head: Stage
What happens
rows: The plaintiff's complaint states the claims; the defendant files an answer admitting or denying them, or a motion to dismiss, for example for failure to state a claim: even if every fact alleged were true, the law gives no remedy.
Each side gets evidence from the other: documents, written questions (interrogatories) and depositions (questioning under oath).
A party asks the judge to decide without trial because there is no genuine dispute about any material fact and it is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.
A jury (or the judge, in a bench trial) hears evidence and decides the facts.
The court enters judgment; the loser may move for a new trial and may appeal.

blocks.html: Each stage is a filter. A motion to dismiss tests the law: if the facts alleged would not win even if proved, why spend money on discovery? Summary judgment tests the evidence: after discovery, if no reasonable jury could find for one side, why hold a trial? A trial is needed only when a real dispute of fact remains. Federal courts follow the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, in effect since 1938; states have similar rules. Settlement happens at every stage: by most estimates well over 90 percent of civil cases end without a trial verdict.

blocks.title: Which stage?
blocks.q: An opinion says: "The district court granted the defendant's motion to dismiss for failure to state a claim. We reverse." What facts did the appellate court assume were true?
steps: A motion to dismiss comes before discovery.
At that stage the court takes the complaint's factual allegations as true and asks whether they state a claim the law recognizes.
Reversal means the claim, if proved, could win; the case returns for discovery.
blocks.a: All the facts alleged in the complaint.

blocks.title: Summary judgment
blocks.q: After discovery, the only evidence is a signed contract and the defendant's admission that he never paid. The defendant offers no evidence of any defense. What should the plaintiff file?
steps: There is no genuine dispute about the material facts.
Under the law of contracts, those facts entitle the plaintiff to judgment.
blocks.a: A motion for summary judgment.

blocks.html: Thinking most lawsuits go to trial. Only a small share of federal civil cases are decided by a trial verdict; most settle or are decided on motions. When you read an appellate case, find the procedural stage first: it tells you whether the court decided what the facts alleged could support (dismissal), what the evidence could support (summary judgment), or what a factfinder found (trial).
This is an educational course, not legal advice.

A criminal case follows its own path, shaped by the Constitution's protections for people accused of crimes. Compare it with the civil path: the parties, the charging documents and the endings all differ.

blocks.name: cv-order
blocks.cap: Put the stages of a criminal case in order, then press Check.

blocks.html: A criminal case moves from investigation and arrest to charging (a grand jury indictment, required for federal felonies, or a prosecutor's information), arraignment and plea, pretrial motions, plea bargaining or trial, sentencing and appeal. Most convictions come from guilty pleas.

Each step reflects a constitutional rule. The Fifth Amendment requires a grand jury indictment for federal "capital, or otherwise infamous" crimes, so a group of citizens, not the prosecutor alone, decides there is probable cause. The Supreme Court has not applied that requirement to the states, and about half the states use grand juries for felonies; others let prosecutors file an information after a preliminary hearing. At trial the government must prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt, and a jury's guilty verdict for a serious crime must be unanimous (Ramos v. Louisiana, 2020). Plea bargaining resolves more than 90 percent of convictions, state and federal: the defendant pleads guilty, often to a lesser charge or for a sentencing recommendation, and gives up the right to trial.

blocks.title: Can the government appeal?
blocks.q: A jury acquits a defendant. The prosecutor believes the judge made a legal error that helped the defense. May the government appeal the acquittal?
steps: The Double Jeopardy Clause bars a second trial for the same offense after an acquittal.
An appeal that could lead to a retrial would put the defendant in jeopardy again, so a jury's acquittal is final.
The defense, by contrast, may appeal a conviction.
blocks.a: No. An acquittal cannot be appealed by the government.

blocks.title: A hung jury
blocks.q: The jury cannot agree, and the judge declares a mistrial. May the state try the defendant again?
steps: A mistrial caused by a hung jury is not an acquittal.
Retrial after a hung jury does not violate double jeopardy.
blocks.a: Yes, the state may retry the case.

blocks.html: Thinking the prosecution can appeal an acquittal. Double jeopardy bars a government appeal of a jury's acquittal; only the defense may appeal a conviction (the government may appeal some rulings made before trial, such as an order suppressing evidence). Check: did the case end in an acquittal? Then it is over for that offense.
This is an educational course, not legal advice.
Every case has a name, and the name is a small map of the dispute. It tells you who sued whom, and often what kind of case it is and how far it has traveled along the path of a case.

A case name lists the parties: Smith v. Jones ("v." for versus, "against"). At trial they are the plaintiff and the defendant (in a criminal case, the government and the defendant). On appeal they are the appellant (who appeals) and the appellee. At the U.S. Supreme Court they are the petitioner (who asked for review) and the respondent.

head: Court
The side that brought this stage
The other side

blocks.html: The names track roles, and roles change as a case moves. Whoever lost below and seeks review becomes the appellant or petitioner, even if that party was the defendant at trial. Courts do not agree on the order of names on appeal. The federal courts of appeals keep the trial court's title, while some state appellate courts put the appealing party first. The U.S. Supreme Court lists the petitioner first. That is why the same case can carry two names. Ernesto Miranda was prosecuted by Arizona, and his case reached the Arizona Supreme Court as State v. Miranda; when he sought review in the U.S. Supreme Court it became Miranda v. Arizona (1966).

items: Criminal cases are brought in the name of the government: United States v. in federal court; State v. in many states; People v. in states such as New York, California, Illinois and Michigan; Commonwealth v. in Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, Virginia and Kentucky.
In re ("in the matter of") names a case without two opposing parties in the usual sense, such as a juvenile or bankruptcy matter: In re Gault (1967).
Courts sometimes use pseudonyms, such as Doe, to protect a party's privacy.

blocks.title: Follow the names
blocks.q: Rosa sues Acme Corp. in federal district court and wins. Acme appeals and loses. Acme petitions the Supreme Court, which grants review. What is the case called at each stage, and who is the petitioner?
steps: District court: Rosa v. Acme Corp. (Rosa is plaintiff).
Court of appeals: still Rosa v. Acme Corp., with Acme as appellant and Rosa as appellee (federal appeals keep the trial title).
Supreme Court: the petitioner comes first, so Acme Corp. v. Rosa.
blocks.a: Rosa v. Acme Corp. below; Acme Corp. v. Rosa in the Supreme Court; Acme is the petitioner.

blocks.name: cv-case

opts.facts: Arizona prosecuted Ernesto Miranda (in the state courts, State v. Miranda). He was convicted, the Arizona Supreme Court affirmed, and he petitioned the U.S. Supreme Court.

blocks.cap: At the Supreme Court the petitioner's name comes first.

blocks.html: Thinking the first name is always the plaintiff. On appeal, many courts put the appealing party first, so the order can flip between courts, as in State v. Miranda and Miranda v. Arizona. Check the court and the stage: at the Supreme Court, the first name is the petitioner, who lost below.
This is an educational course, not legal advice.

Lawyers point to cases with citations, compact addresses that tell you where to find the opinion in a printed series of books called a reporter. Learning to read one takes a minute and saves hours. It builds on case names.

blocks.name: cv-case
blocks.cap: Brown v. Board of Education, 347 U.S. 483 (1954).

blocks.html: In Brown v. Board of Education, 347 U.S. 483 (1954): 347 is the volume, U.S. is the reporter (United States Reports, the Supreme Court's official reporter), 483 is the first page of the opinion, and 1954 is the year of decision.

head: Reporter
Abbreviation
Which courts
rows: Supreme Court (unofficial, often cited alongside, as parallel citations)
U.S. courts of appeals (F.3d ran from 1993 to 2021; F.4th since 2021)
F. Supp., F. Supp. 2d, F. Supp. 3d

blocks.html: Before databases, the only way to find an opinion was by its book and page, and the system still works the same way online. The order is always volume, reporter, page. A citation to a specific passage adds a pinpoint page after a comma: Brown, 347 U.S. at 495, points to page 495, where the Court held that separate schools are inherently unequal. For lower courts, the parentheses also name the court, because the reporter alone does not say which circuit or district decided the case: "(9th Cir. 2018)" or "(S.D.N.Y. 2019)". The earliest Supreme Court volumes were named for their private reporters, so Marbury v. Madison is cited 5 U.S. (1 Cranch) 137 (1803): volume 5 of the U.S. Reports, which is volume 1 of Cranch's reports.

blocks.title: Read it aloud
blocks.q: What does "Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555, 560 (1992)" tell you?
steps: Volume 504 of the United States Reports, so a Supreme Court case.
The opinion begins on page 555.
The 560 is a pinpoint: the passage cited is on page 560.
Decided in 1992.
blocks.a: A 1992 Supreme Court case in volume 504 of U.S. Reports, starting at page 555, citing page 560.

blocks.title: Which court?
blocks.q: An invented citation: "Park v. Lane, 41 F.4th 210 (7th Cir. 2022)." Which court decided it?
steps: F.4th is the Federal Reporter, Fourth Series: the U.S. courts of appeals.
The parenthetical names the Seventh Circuit.
blocks.a: The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit, in 2022.

blocks.html: Reading the first number as a case number or a page. The number before the reporter is the volume; the number after it is the first page. Check: a citation like "347 U.S. 483" never means page 347. Also, the year in parentheses is when the case was decided, not when it was filed.
This is an educational course, not legal advice.
Open a Supreme Court decision found by its citation and you will meet several documents bound together. Knowing which is which keeps you from quoting the wrong one.

A decision may include a syllabus (a summary that is not part of the opinion), the opinion of the Court (the majority's reasoning, which states the law), concurring opinions (agreeing with the result, sometimes for different reasons), dissenting opinions and, when no reasoning wins a majority, a plurality opinion.

head: Part
Who writes it
Is it law?
rows: the Reporter of Decisions, for the reader's convenience
no: it "constitutes no part of the opinion of the Court"
a justice for a majority (or "per curiam," unsigned, for the Court)
a justice who joins the majority but adds views
no, but it may shape later readings
a justice who agrees only with the result
no, though in split decisions it can matter
a justice who disagrees with the result
no, but some dissents later become the majority view
the largest group when no reasoning has five votes
limited: lower courts look for the narrowest common ground

blocks.html: The Court speaks as a body only when a majority agrees on the reasoning. The syllabus comes first in the book, but every Supreme Court slip opinion carries the note that "the syllabus constitutes no part of the opinion of the Court but has been prepared by the Reporter of Decisions for the convenience of the reader," citing United States v. Detroit Timber & Lumber Co., 200 U.S. 321, 337 (1906). Separate opinions matter because they show the limits of a holding and the arguments for its future. Justice Robert Jackson's concurrence in Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer (1952) became the leading framework for presidential power, and Justice John Marshall Harlan's lone dissent in Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) is now far better known than the majority. When a decision has only a plurality, Marks v. United States (1977) tells lower courts to treat the position of the justices who concurred in the judgment on the narrowest grounds as the holding.

blocks.title: Count the votes
blocks.q: Five justices join an opinion by Justice A. Justice B writes separately, "concurring in the judgment." Justices C, D and E dissent. Is A's opinion the opinion of the Court? What is the vote?
steps: Five justices joined A's reasoning: a majority of nine, so it is the opinion of the Court.
B agrees with the result only, so the judgment has six votes.
Three dissent.
blocks.a: Yes; the judgment is 6–3, and A's opinion is a majority opinion.

blocks.title: A plurality
blocks.q: Four justices join an opinion reversing on ground X. Two justices concur in the judgment on ground Y. Three dissent. Is there an opinion of the Court?
steps: Six votes to reverse, so the judgment is reversed.
But no single reasoning has five votes: four for X, two for Y.
The four-justice opinion is a plurality opinion; lower courts look for the narrowest ground the majority shares.
blocks.a: No. The judgment is 6–3, announced in a plurality opinion.

In U.S. Reports the syllabus is prepared by the Reporter of Decisions and is not part of the opinion; headnotes added by publishers are not either. blocks.html: Law students prepare for class by writing a case brief: a one-page summary of an opinion in a fixed form. (It is not the same as the long "brief" a lawyer files with a court.) Once you know the parts of an opinion, briefing is a way of pulling out the parts that matter.
A student case brief records the facts, the procedural history, the issue (the question presented), the holding, the reasoning and the disposition, and often notes concurrences and dissents.

head: Heading
What to write
rows: only the facts the court relied on, in a few sentences
what the lower courts did and how the case got here
the legal question, as a yes-or-no question tied to the facts
the answer to the issue, as a rule ("Yes; a plaintiff who…")
why the court decided as it did: the rule's source and how it applied
the main point of any concurrence or dissent

blocks.html: Briefing forces you to decide what the case stands for. Copying passages is easy; stating the issue in one question and the holding in one sentence takes understanding. A good test: the holding should answer the issue exactly, and the reasoning should explain why the answer is yes or no. Your brief is also a tool for telling holding from dicta: anything that does not help answer the issue belongs elsewhere.
