opts.facts: A federal regulation limited a consultation duty under the Endangered Species Act to agency actions in the United States or on the high seas. Wildlife groups sued. Two members said they had visited project areas abroad (in Egypt and Sri Lanka) to see endangered species and hoped to return someday.
opts.reasoning: Article III requires an injury in fact that is concrete and imminent. "Someday" plans to return, with no concrete plans, are not imminent injury. The Court also rejected standing based only on a procedural violation that caused the plaintiffs no concrete harm.
opts.later: Its three-part test for standing is quoted in nearly every standing case.

blocks.cap: A brief of Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife (1992). Reveal each part in turn.

blocks.title: Write the issue
blocks.q: Turn this vague issue into a good one: "Standing."
steps: Make it a yes-or-no question.
Tie it to the key facts: members who visited habitats abroad and hoped to return someday.
Name the legal standard: injury in fact under Article III.
blocks.a: Do members of a group who once visited endangered species' habitats abroad and intend to return "someday" suffer an injury in fact that gives them standing under Article III?

blocks.title: Match the holding
blocks.q: Write the holding for that issue.
steps: Answer the question directly.
Keep the key facts and the rule.
blocks.a: No. Vague "someday" intentions to return, without concrete plans, do not show an actual or imminent injury, so the plaintiffs lacked standing.

blocks.html: Copying long passages and missing the issue. Write the issue as a yes-or-no question that the holding answers. Check your brief: if the holding does not begin with "yes" or "no" (or a clear rule) that answers your issue, one of them is wrong.

blocks.name: cv-order
blocks.cap: Put the headings of a case brief in the usual order.

blocks.html: This is an educational course, not legal advice.
A case brief summarizes how a court reasoned. IRAC is how you reason yourself, on an exam, in a memo, or in your head when a new problem arrives.

IRAC organizes legal analysis: state the Issue, the Rule, the Application of the rule to the facts and the Conclusion. The Application, where each element of the rule is matched to specific facts, does most of the work.

A legal question is answered by a rule applied to facts, so the analysis has a natural order: what question, what rule, how the rule fits these facts, and so what. IRAC makes that order visible to the reader (a professor, a partner, a judge), who can check each step. The Application is where cases are won: anyone can recite a rule, but showing that these facts do or do not satisfy each element takes care. Many writers use variants, such as CREAC (Conclusion, Rule, Explanation, Application, Conclusion), which put the answer first; the logic is the same.

blocks.name: cv-case

opts.name: The skateboard ordinance (an invented problem)
opts.facts: A city ordinance says: "No person shall ride a skateboard on a public sidewalk in the downtown district." Jo rode a skateboard across a private parking lot downtown, then stepped onto the sidewalk carrying the board.
opts.test: A violation requires (1) riding (2) a skateboard (3) on a public sidewalk (4) in the downtown district.
opts.reasoning: Jo did ride a skateboard downtown (elements 1, 2 and 4 for the parking lot), but the lot is private, not a public sidewalk. On the sidewalk, Jo carried the board and did not ride it. No moment satisfies all four elements at once.
opts.holding: No. Jo did not violate the ordinance.

blocks.cap: IRAC on a small problem. Reveal each part.

blocks.title: Tie each element to a fact
blocks.q: Rule: a battery is an intentional act that causes a harmful or offensive contact with another person. Facts: as a prank, Max pulled a chair away as Nell sat down, and she hit the floor. Apply IRAC.
steps: Issue: Did Max commit a battery?
Rule: intent to cause the contact (or knowledge it will almost certainly happen), and a harmful or offensive contact results.
Application: Max knew Nell was about to sit, so he knew she would almost certainly hit the floor. Her contact with the floor was harmful, and his act caused it, even though he never touched her.
Conclusion: Yes, Max likely committed a battery.
blocks.a: Yes: each element is matched to a fact.

blocks.title: An honest mistake
blocks.q: Rule: a person commits the tort of trespass to land by intentionally entering land in another's possession without permission. Facts: a hiker crosses an unmarked boundary into a private field, sure she is still in a state forest. Apply IRAC.
steps: Issue: Is the hiker liable for trespass when she believed the land was public?
Rule: the intent required is the intent to enter that place; in tort law, a mistake about who owns it is not a defense.
Application: she meant to walk where she walked, and the field was in another's possession without permission. Her belief that it was public goes to the wrong question.
Conclusion: she likely committed trespass, though with no harm done the owner may recover only nominal damages.
blocks.a: Yes, likely trespass: the element is intent to enter, not knowledge of ownership.

blocks.name: cv-sort

cards.text: Was the contract formed when Lee replied "Deal"?
A contract requires an offer, an acceptance and consideration.
Lee's "Deal" accepted Kim's offer to sell the bike for \$90.
So a contract was formed.

blocks.cap: Sort the sentences of a short analysis.

blocks.html: Stating the rule and jumping to the conclusion. Without the application, the analysis is only a guess. Tie each element of the rule to specific facts, and say what is missing when an element fails. Check: can a reader point to the fact that satisfies each element you listed?
This is an educational course, not legal advice.

The last line of an appellate opinion, the disposition, says what happens to the lower court's decision. It is short, but you need it to know who won and what comes next. It is part of every opinion and every case brief.

An appellate court may affirm (leave the decision in place), reverse (overturn it), vacate (set it aside) or remand (send the case back for more proceedings). Courts often combine them: "reversed and remanded," "vacated and remanded," "affirmed in part and reversed in part."

head: Disposition
Meaning
What happens next
rows: the case is over at this level (the loser may seek further review)
the lower court reached the wrong result
often with a remand to enter a new judgment or hold further proceedings
the judgment is set aside, often because the lower court used the wrong legal standard
usually remanded to decide again under the right standard; the outcome may end up the same
sent back to the lower court
the lower court acts under the appellate court's instructions
the judgment is changed in part

blocks.html: Appellate courts correct legal errors, but they usually do not find facts or hold trials. So when an error matters, they often cannot simply declare a winner: they send the case back for the trial court to finish the job correctly. Vacating is the tool when the lower court used the wrong test but the appellate court cannot tell how the case would come out under the right one. The Supreme Court sometimes grants review, vacates and remands in one order (a "GVR") so a lower court can reconsider in light of a new decision.

blocks.title: Reversed, but not over
blocks.q: A trial court dismissed Ray's suit, ruling that the defendant owed him no duty. The court of appeals holds that the defendant did owe a duty and writes "Reversed and remanded." Has Ray won?
steps: Reversal undoes the dismissal.
Remand sends the case back for further proceedings.
Ray still must prove breach, causation and damages.
blocks.a: No. He has won only the right to continue his case.

blocks.title: Vacated
blocks.q: The court of appeals finds that the trial judge used the wrong legal test but cannot tell whether the result would differ. What disposition fits?
steps: It cannot say the result was wrong, so "reversed" is too strong.
It sets the judgment aside and asks the trial court to decide again under the right test.
blocks.a: Vacated and remanded.

blocks.name: cv-court
blocks.cap: A remand sends the case back down to the court below.

blocks.html: Thinking "reversed" means the other side wins the whole case. A reversal often comes with a remand, and the case continues in the lower court. Check the full disposition line and the last paragraph of the opinion, which usually says what the lower court should do next.
This is an educational course, not legal advice.
In IRAC you applied a rule to facts. Underneath, that is an old form of argument from logic. If you have met modus ponens on the Logic Ladder, you already know its shape: if P then Q; P; therefore Q.

Applying a rule is a deductive argument, often called a legal syllogism: the rule is the major premise, the facts are the minor premise, and the result follows. Most legal disputes are not about the logic but about the premises: which rule applies, what it means, and what the facts are.

head: Part
Logic
Law
rows: Anyone who takes another's property without consent, intending to keep it, commits theft.
Kim took Lee's bicycle without consent, intending to keep it.

blocks.html: Why frame law this way? Because it makes the reasoning checkable. If the premises are true and the form is valid, the conclusion must follow, so anyone who rejects the conclusion has to say which premise is wrong. That points the argument where it belongs. A valid argument can still be unsound if a premise is false. So lawyers rarely attack the form. They attack the major premise (that is not the rule here, or the rule means something else) or the minor premise (that is not what happened, or that fact does not fit the rule's words).

blocks.title: Where is the fight?
blocks.q: Rule: "No vehicles in the park." Facts: Ada rode a bicycle through the park. Conclusion: Ada violated the rule. The syllogism looks valid. Where will the argument be?
steps: The form is fine: if a vehicle is in the park, the rule is broken; a vehicle was in the park.
But the minor premise hides a question: is a bicycle a "vehicle" under this rule?
That is a question about the rule's meaning, not about logic. (Legal philosophers have used this "no vehicles in the park" example since H. L. A. Hart used it in 1958.)
blocks.a: Over the meaning of "vehicle," a premise, not the logic.

blocks.title: Affirming the consequent
blocks.q: A lawyer argues: "Anyone who commits burglary enters a building. My client's neighbor entered the building. So the neighbor committed burglary." What is wrong?
steps: The rule says burglary → entry, not entry → burglary.
Inferring the "if" part from the "then" part is the fallacy of affirming the consequent.
Many people enter buildings lawfully.
blocks.a: The argument is invalid: it affirms the consequent.

blocks.name: cv-order

items: Rule: a person who signs a guarantee must pay the debt if the borrower does not.
Facts: Sal signed a guarantee, and the borrower did not pay.
Conclusion: Sal must pay the debt.

blocks.cap: Put the syllogism in order: major premise, minor premise, conclusion.

blocks.name: cv-sort

cards.text: The statute was repealed before the act.
My client was in another city that night.
"Vehicle" in this rule means motor vehicles only.
The witness could not have seen the color of the light.

blocks.cap: Two ways to resist a legal syllogism.

blocks.html: Thinking a valid legal syllogism settles a case. The form may be valid, but each premise can be contested: the rule's existence and meaning, and the facts and how they are described. Check: when you lay out a syllogism, ask of each premise, "could the other side deny this?" That is where the case will be argued.
This is an educational course, not legal advice.

sources.name: Frederick Schauer, "A Critical Guide to Vehicles in the Park," 83 N.Y.U. Law Review 1109 (2008)

blocks.html: Deduction works when the rule is clear. But often the rule lives in earlier cases, and the question is whether a new case is enough like them. That is reasoning by analogy, the method at the heart of the common law. You may know the general form from arguments from analogy on the Logic Ladder; it builds on rules as syllogisms.

Lawyers argue that a case is like a precedent in the ways that matter (analogizing) or unlike it (distinguishing). The key is to identify which facts are material: the facts that mattered to the earlier court's reasons.

Like cases should be treated alike, but every two cases are alike in some ways and different in others. Two cases may both happen on a Tuesday; that does not matter. They may both involve a defendant who knew of a danger; that may matter a great deal. The earlier court's reasons tell you which similarities count. So an analogy has three steps: (1) find the reason the precedent gave; (2) find the facts that reason depended on; (3) ask whether the new case shares those facts.

blocks.name: cv-case

opts.name: Hale v. Ortiz (an invented precedent)
opts.facts: Ortiz kept a dog that had bitten two people before. Ortiz knew this, left the gate open, and the dog bit Hale.
opts.q: Is an owner liable for a bite by a dog the owner knew was dangerous?
opts.holding: Yes. An owner who knows an animal is dangerous and fails to restrain it is liable for the harm.
opts.reasoning: The owner's knowledge of the danger, plus the failure to control it, makes it fair to put the loss on the owner.

blocks.cap: An invented precedent. Which of its facts were material?

blocks.title: Analogize
blocks.q: New case: Vic keeps a goat that has butted and injured three visitors, and Vic knows it. Vic leaves the pen open, and the goat injures Wren. Does Hale v. Ortiz help Wren?
steps: Reason in Hale: knowledge of the animal's danger plus failure to restrain it.
Here: Vic knew of the danger (three injuries) and failed to restrain the goat (open pen).
That it is a goat, not a dog, does not touch the reason.
blocks.a: Yes. The material facts match; Wren analogizes to Hale.

blocks.title: Distinguish
blocks.q: New case: Uma's dog had never bitten or threatened anyone. It slipped its leash and bit Tam. Does Hale control?
steps: Hale turned on the owner's knowledge of a dangerous animal.
Uma had no reason to know her dog was dangerous.
Both cases involve a dog bite, but that is a surface likeness.
blocks.a: Uma can distinguish Hale: the material fact of knowledge is missing (Tam may need another theory, such as negligence or a statute).

blocks.name: cv-sort

cards.text: The owner knew the animal had hurt people before
The animal was a dog
The owner left the gate open
The bite happened on a Tuesday
The victim's name was Hale

blocks.cap: Sort the facts of the precedent.

blocks.html: Comparing cases on surface facts (both involve dogs). Ask what features the earlier court relied on, then whether the new case shares them. A strong analogy matches the reasons, not the props. Check: could you change this fact without changing the earlier court's reasoning? If so, it is not material.
This is an educational course, not legal advice.

Lawmakers and judges choose not only what the law says but how it says it. Some laws draw bright lines; others call for judgment. The choice shapes how cases are argued and decided, and it connects to reasoning by analogy, which standards depend on most.

A rule draws a bright line ("speed limit 65"). A standard calls for judgment ("drive at a reasonable speed for conditions"). Rules are predictable and cheap to apply but can misfit unusual cases; standards fit cases better but are less predictable and give more discretion to whoever applies them.

head: Subject
A rule
A standard
rows: no faster than is reasonable for conditions
a person mature enough to vote
suit must be filed within two years (a statute of limitations)
suit must be filed without unreasonable delay
stop fully at every stop sign
act as a reasonable person would

blocks.html: Every rule is over-inclusive and under-inclusive compared with its purpose. A voting age of 18 excludes some mature 17-year-olds and includes some immature 30-year-olds. But it is easy to apply, treats everyone alike, and leaves little room for bias or error. A standard aims straight at the purpose (maturity, reasonable speed), but people cannot know in advance exactly what it requires, and different judges may apply it differently. Legal scholars have long debated the trade-off; Justice Antonin Scalia, for example, defended rules in "The Rule of Law as a Law of Rules" (1989), and Kathleen Sullivan described how justices divide between rules and standards in a 1992 Harvard Law Review foreword. Most areas of law use both, and some start as standards and harden into rules as cases accumulate.

blocks.title: Rule or standard?
blocks.q: Classify: (a) "A will must be signed by two witnesses." (b) "A parent must act in the best interests of the child." (c) "A contract for the sale of land must be in writing."
steps: (a) A bright line: count the signatures. Rule.
(b) Requires judgment about many circumstances. Standard.
(c) A bright line: is there a writing? Rule.
blocks.a: (a) rule, (b) standard, (c) rule.

blocks.title: The cost of a rule
blocks.q: A city bans "any dog over 50 pounds" from a crowded festival to prevent bites. Name one way the rule is over-inclusive and one way it is under-inclusive.
steps: Over-inclusive: a calm, trained 60-pound service-type dog is banned though it poses little risk.
Under-inclusive: an aggressive 40-pound dog is allowed though it poses real risk.
A standard ("no dangerous dogs") would fit better but would be harder to enforce at the gate.
blocks.a: It bans some safe dogs and admits some dangerous ones.

blocks.name: cv-sort

cards.text: No one under 16 may drive
Use reasonable care
Quiet hours are 10 p.m. to 7 a.m.
No unreasonable noise
Bail may not be excessive
Senators must be at least 30 years old

blocks.cap: Sort each provision.

blocks.html: Thinking one form is always better. Each has costs and benefits; much of law is the choice between them. Check by asking two questions: (1) how costly are mistakes at the edges? (2) how much do we value knowing the answer in advance? High value on predictability favors a rule; high cost of misfit favors a standard.
This is an educational course, not legal advice.

sources.name: Antonin Scalia, "The Rule of Law as a Law of Rules," 56 University of Chicago Law Review 1175 (1989)
Kathleen M. Sullivan, "Foreword: The Justices of Rules and Standards," 106 Harvard Law Review 22 (1992)

blocks.html: Legal rules and standards are often written as tests with several parts. Before applying one, you must know what kind of test it is, because the parts combine in different ways.

An element test lists parts that all must be proven; if one fails, the claim fails. A factor test lists considerations to weigh together; none is decisive by itself. A balancing test weighs competing interests against each other.

head: Kind
Example
How it works
rows: all four must be proven; missing any one ends the claim
copyright fair use: the purpose of the use, the nature of the work, how much was used, the effect on the market (17 U.S.C. § 107)
the court weighs all four together; a use can be fair even if one factor points the other way
Mathews v. Eldridge (1976): what process is due is found by weighing the private interest, the risk of error and the value of more safeguards, and the government's interest
the interests are set against each other

blocks.html: Element tests make a claim a chain: it is only as strong as its weakest link. That gives a defendant a clear target: knock out one element and you win. Factor and balancing tests reflect judgments that many things matter and none should be decisive alone. They resemble standards: flexible, but less predictable. The tiers of scrutiny in constitutional law are a structured kind of test: a court first classifies the law, then asks how strong the government's interest is and how well the law fits it.

blocks.title: One element missing
blocks.q: A negligence claim: the driver owed a duty, ran a red light (breach), and hit the plaintiff's car. But the plaintiff's car was parked and empty, and there was no damage at all. Does the claim succeed?
steps: Negligence is an element test: duty, breach, causation, damages.
Duty, breach and causation of contact are present.
No damage: the damages element fails.
blocks.a: No. Without damages, the claim fails, however careless the driver was.

blocks.title: Weigh the factors
blocks.q: A teacher copies one short poem from a long anthology for a class discussion. One fair use factor (the nature of the work: creative) leans against fair use. Is the use necessarily unfair?
steps: Fair use is a factor test.
Purpose (teaching, nonprofit) leans toward fair use; amount (one short poem) leans toward it; market effect may be small.
One factor against is not decisive; the court weighs them together.
blocks.a: No. The other factors may outweigh it.

blocks.name: cv-scrutiny
blocks.cap: A structured test you will meet in constitutional law: the three tiers of scrutiny, each with an interest and a fit requirement.

blocks.html: Treating factor tests like element tests, and stopping when one factor fails. In a factor test the court weighs them all together. Check the source of the test: words like "must prove each of the following" signal elements; words like "courts consider" or "factors include" signal factors.
This is an educational course, not legal advice.

sources.name: Mathews v. Eldridge, 424 U.S. 319 (1976) (no Grokipedia page)

blocks.html: Every element of a test must be proven by someone, to some level of certainty. Those are two different questions: who must prove it, and how sure the factfinder must be. You met the two main standards in civil and criminal cases.

The burden of proof says which party must prove a point. It has two parts: the burden of production (offering enough evidence to put the issue in play) and the burden of persuasion (convincing the factfinder). The standard says how sure the factfinder must be: a preponderance of the evidence (more likely than not), clear and convincing evidence, or beyond a reasonable doubt.

blocks.name: cv-order
blocks.cap: Order the standards from least to most demanding.

head: Standard
Meaning
Typical use
rows: more likely true than not (just over 50 percent)
highly probable; well above a preponderance
some civil matters, such as fraud claims in many states, involuntary commitment, and defamation of a public figure (for actual malice)
no reasonable doubt of guilt remains; the highest standard
every element of a crime (In re Winship, 1970)

blocks.html: The burden decides close cases: if the evidence is evenly balanced, the party with the burden of persuasion loses. That is why who bears it matters so much. The standard reflects how costly each kind of error is. In an ordinary civil case, a wrong verdict for either side is about equally bad, so the law asks only which account is more likely. Where liberty or reputation is at stake, the law accepts more wrong acquittals to avoid wrong convictions, so it raises the bar. Courts avoid putting numbers on the higher standards; "50 percent" is only a way to explain the preponderance tie-breaker.

blocks.title: A tie
blocks.q: In a civil case, the jury thinks the plaintiff's and the defendant's versions are exactly equally likely. Who wins?
steps: The plaintiff bears the burden of persuasion on her claim.
Preponderance requires her version to be more likely than not.
A tie is not more likely than not.
blocks.a: The defendant wins.

blocks.title: Same evidence, different results
blocks.q: A jury believes it is about 70 percent likely that Drew caused a fire on purpose. What results in (1) a criminal arson trial and (2) a civil suit by the building owner?
steps: (1) Seventy percent leaves a real doubt; that is not proof beyond a reasonable doubt. Acquittal.
(2) Seventy percent is more likely than not. The owner wins.
blocks.a: (1) not guilty; (2) liable.

blocks.html: Thinking "preponderance" means a large majority of the evidence, or more witnesses. It means more likely true than not, even by a slight margin, and it is about the convincing force of the evidence, not its amount. One believable witness can outweigh three who are not. Check: would the factfinder say "more likely than not"? Then the preponderance standard is met.
This is an educational course, not legal advice.

Most modern law is written by legislatures, through the process you met in how a bill becomes law. So much of a lawyer's work is reading statutes and arguing about what they mean. This unit covers the tools. Every method starts in the same place: the words. You will use IRAC to apply what you find.

Courts begin with the statute's text, read in its ordinary meaning at the time it was enacted and in the context of the whole statute. If the meaning is clear, most judges stop there. Textualists hold that the enacted words are the law.

The text is what passed both houses of Congress and was signed by the President (or passed over a veto). Under Article I, only that text became law; private hopes of its authors did not. Reading words as an ordinary reader would at the time also gives fair notice: people can plan by the law's words. Context matters because words take meaning from their surroundings: "bank" means one thing in a banking act and another in a law about rivers. Courts use dictionaries as evidence of ordinary meaning, read defined terms by the statute's own definitions, and give terms of art (words with a settled legal meaning) that technical meaning.

blocks.title: Is a tomato a vegetable?
blocks.q: An 1883 tariff taxed imported vegetables but not fruits. An importer argued tomatoes are botanically fruits. In Nix v. Hedden (1893), how did the Supreme Court decide?
steps: The statute used ordinary words for trade, not scientific terms.
In common speech, tomatoes were served and sold as vegetables.
So "vegetables" in the statute included tomatoes.
blocks.a: Tomatoes were vegetables under the act: ordinary meaning governed.

blocks.title: Is an airplane a vehicle?
blocks.q: A 1919 federal law punished taking a stolen "motor vehicle" across state lines, defining it to include "any other self-propelled vehicle not designed for running on rails." In McBoyle v. United States (1931), the defendant had flown a stolen airplane. Did the law apply?
steps: In everyday speech of the time, "vehicle" called up things that move on land.
The list in the definition (automobiles, trucks, motorcycles and the like) pointed the same way.
Justice Holmes wrote for the Court that a criminal law should give fair warning in words a common reader would understand.
blocks.a: No. The Court held an airplane was not a "vehicle" under that statute.

blocks.name: cv-doc

doc.title: An invented park ordinance
doc.source: For practice; not a real law
paras: Section 1. No vehicle may be driven or parked in any city park.
Section 2. In this ordinance, "vehicle" means any device in, upon, or by which any person or property may be transported on land, except devices moved by human power.

marks.text: No vehicle may be driven or parked
marks.note: The operative rule: what is forbidden.
A definition section. The statute's own definition controls over a dictionary.

marks.text: except devices moved by human power
marks.note: So bicycles and strollers are outside the rule, whatever a dictionary says.

blocks.cap: Read the definitions before reaching for a dictionary. Tap the marked phrases.

blocks.html: Some general rules of reading are set by statute too: the federal Dictionary Act (1 U.S.C. § 1) says, for example, that unless context shows otherwise, words in the singular include the plural.

Thinking textualism means reading each word alone, as in a dictionary. Textualists read words in context, as a skilled reader of the whole statute would understand them at the time of enactment: definitions, neighboring words, the structure of the act and settled legal meanings all count. Check: before deciding what a word means, read the whole section and the definitions.
This is an educational course, not legal advice.

sources.name: Frederick Schauer, "A Critical Guide to Vehicles in the Park," 83 N.Y.U. Law Review 1109 (2008)

blocks.html: What should a court do when the plain words are unclear, or when a literal reading would produce a result no one could have wanted? One answer, with a long history, is to ask what the statute is for.

Purposivists read a statute in light of the problem it was meant to solve and its evident purpose, especially when the words are unclear or a literal reading would defeat the statute's aims. They start with the text too; they differ from textualists in how much weight purpose gets.

Legislatures pass laws to accomplish goals, and words are imperfect tools. A reader who knows the goal can often see which of two possible meanings fits. The idea is old: in Heydon's Case (1584) an English court said judges should ask what "mischief" (problem) the statute addressed and how it meant to remedy it. In the United States, Henry Hart and Albert Sacks's teaching materials The Legal Process (1958) urged judges to treat statutes as the work of reasonable people pursuing reasonable purposes. Purposivists argue that this makes statutes work as intended and respects the legislature better than a wooden reading would. Textualists answer that purposes are often stated at a high level, that every statute is a compromise that pursues its purpose only so far, and that the words are the best evidence of how far.

blocks.title: Church of the Holy Trinity v. United States (1892)
blocks.q: A federal law banned paying the passage of a foreigner to come to the United States to perform "labor or service of any kind." A church in New York paid for an English minister to come be its rector. Did the church violate the law?
steps: Read literally, a minister's work is "service of any kind."
The Court looked at the title of the act, the evil it targeted (contracts for cheap manual labor) and its history.
It concluded Congress did not mean to reach a church hiring a pastor, and said a thing may be within the letter of a statute yet not within its spirit.
blocks.a: No. The Court read the law by its purpose, not its broadest literal sense. (Textualists often cite this case as an example of what to avoid.)

blocks.title: An absurd result
blocks.q: A city ordinance says "No one may sleep in the train station." A traveler dozes for ten minutes in a chair waiting for a late train; a person sets up a bed for the night. How might a purposivist and a textualist read the ordinance?
steps: Purposivist: the ordinance targets using the station as a place to spend the night, so the dozing traveler is outside it and the overnight sleeper is inside.

Textualist: "sleep" in ordinary meaning covers both, but a textualist may also ask whether the context (a station rule) shows "sleep" means bedding down there; most textualists accept a narrow absurdity exception.
Both reach the overnight sleeper; they may differ on the traveler and on how they get there.
blocks.a: The overnight sleeper is covered under either approach; the methods differ at the edges.

blocks.name: cv-sort

cards.text: The ordinary meaning of "service" when the law was passed included a minister's work.
The act was aimed at importing cheap manual labor.
Only the enacted words went through both houses and the President.
A reading that defeats the statute's goal cannot be what the legislature meant.

blocks.cap: Sort the arguments about the Holy Trinity statute.

blocks.html: Thinking purposivists ignore the text. Purposivists start with the text too; they differ in how much weight purpose gets when the text is unclear or leads to an odd result. Check by asking each side: "what would change your mind?" A textualist points to the words; a purposivist points to the words read in light of the goal.
This is an educational course, not legal advice.

sources.name: Grokipedia, "Church of the Holy Trinity v. United States"
Frederick Schauer, "A Critical Guide to Vehicles in the Park," 83 N.Y.U. Law Review 1109 (2008)

blocks.html: If purpose matters, where do you find it? One place is the record of how the statute was made. Its use is among the most debated questions in statutory interpretation.

Legislative history includes committee reports, floor statements, hearings and earlier drafts of a bill. Its supporters say it shows what Congress meant and what problem it addressed; its critics say only the enacted text was voted on and history can be selective.

head: Kind of history
Weight courts that use it usually give
rows: the most: they explain a bill to the whole chamber before the vote
Statements by a bill's sponsor or floor manager
Changes between drafts (words added or dropped)
Statements made after the law was passed

blocks.html: The case for legislative history: Congress works through committees, and members rely on committee reports to know what a bill does. Reading them helps a court see the problem and the meaning of technical terms, the way you would read the notes of a meeting to understand its decision. Justice Stephen Breyer defended this use in a 1992 article. The case against: under Article I, only the text passed both houses and was presented to the President; reports are written by staff and committee members and are never voted on; and a long record contains statements on every side, so a judge can pick the ones that support the result he wants. Justice Antonin Scalia made these arguments for decades. Courts today vary: some consult history only if the text is unclear; others use it more freely; textualists rarely rely on it.

blocks.title: Weigh the evidence
blocks.q: A statute's meaning is unclear. The Senate committee report says the word "facility" covers mobile units. One senator said on the floor that it does not. A House member said so in a press interview a year after enactment. Which evidence would a court that uses history weigh most?
steps: The committee report explains the bill to the Senate before the vote: heavy weight.
One senator's floor remark: some, but less.
A statement after enactment did not inform anyone's vote: little or none.
blocks.a: The committee report.

blocks.title: A dropped word
blocks.q: A draft of a bill covered "employees and contractors." Before passage, "and contractors" was struck. The enacted law covers "employees." Does the change help someone arguing the law does not cover contractors?
steps: Courts often treat deliberate changes between drafts as meaningful.
Striking "contractors" suggests Congress chose not to cover them.
A textualist might reach the same answer from the word "employees" alone.
blocks.a: Yes, it supports that reading.

blocks.name: cv-order
blocks.cap: Order from most to least weight, as courts that use legislative history usually do.

blocks.html: Treating any statement in the record as Congress's intent. Courts that use history give committee reports more weight than a single member's floor remark, and almost none to statements after enactment. Check: who said it, when, and did the members voting on the bill have it before them?
This is an educational course, not legal advice.

blocks.html: Judges of every school use canons of construction: rules of thumb about how language usually works. The textual canons refine the search for ordinary meaning. Several have Latin names, and you will see them in opinions.

head: Canon
Meaning
Example
rows: listing some things implies the exclusion of others
"Dogs, cats and rabbits may be kept" suggests ferrets may not
general words after a list of specific ones take the list's kind
"cars, trucks, motorcycles and other vehicles": vehicles like those, not airplanes
an unclear word takes meaning from its neighbors
in "tacks, nails and staples," "staples" means fasteners, not basic foods
read every word to do some work; avoid readings that make words pointless
if "sell" already covers "give," why did the law say "sell or give"?
read a provision with the whole statute; the same word usually means the same thing throughout
"employee" in section 2 and section 9 means the same

blocks.html: Textual canons are rules of thumb about language: expressio unius, ejusdem generis, noscitur a sociis, the rule against surplusage and the whole-act rule. They are presumptions, not commands: context can overcome them.

The canons describe how careful writers and readers usually use words. If a drafter wanted to reach everything, why list specifics? If two words meant the same thing, why use both? Applying a canon is a way of asking what an ordinary, attentive reader would take the words to mean. But canons can point in different directions. In a famous 1950 article Karl Llewellyn paired canons that seemed to contradict each other ("thrust" and "parry"). Defenders reply that canons are tools for weighing evidence of meaning, not formulas.

blocks.title: Is a fish a "tangible object"?
blocks.q: A federal law punishes anyone who destroys "any record, document, or tangible object" to obstruct a federal investigation. A fisherman threw undersized fish overboard. In Yates v. United States (2015), did the law reach the fish?
steps: A fish is a tangible object in ordinary speech.

But four justices (the plurality) applied noscitur a sociis and ejusdem generis: "tangible object" sits beside "record" and "document," so it means objects used to record or preserve information. Justice Alito agreed with the result on similar grounds.
Four justices dissented, reading "tangible object" in its ordinary, broad sense.
blocks.a: No, 5–4: the fish were not "tangible objects" under that provision.

blocks.title: Apply ejusdem generis
blocks.q: A park rule bans "skateboards, roller skates, scooters and other wheeled devices." Does it ban a child's wagon? A wheelchair?
steps: The list names things people ride for recreation or travel on small wheels.
"Other wheeled devices" takes that kind: ridden recreation devices.
A wheelchair is a mobility aid, a different kind; a wagon is pulled, not ridden, so it is a closer question.
blocks.a: The wheelchair is likely outside the rule; the wagon is arguable.

blocks.name: cv-sort

cards.text: The law lists three exemptions; a fourth is not implied.
"Pistols, revolvers and other firearms" covers handguns like those named.
"Bark" in "the tree's roots, bark and leaves" is not a dog's bark.
"Willfully and knowingly" must mean more than "knowingly."

blocks.cap: Match each argument to its canon.

blocks.html: Applying ejusdem generis to any list. It applies when general words follow specific ones ("cars, trucks and other vehicles") and limits the general words to that kind. A list with no catch-all at the end calls for expressio unius or noscitur a sociis instead. Check: is there a general catch-all phrase after the list?

blocks.html: The textual canons are about language. A second family, the substantive canons, are about values the legal system protects. They tell a court which way to lean when a statute is unclear.

Substantive canons reflect legal values: the rule of lenity (read unclear criminal laws in the defendant's favor), constitutional avoidance (prefer a fair reading that avoids serious constitutional doubts) and clear-statement rules (Congress must speak clearly to do certain things, such as override a state's sovereign immunity).

head: Canon
What it protects
When it applies
rows: fair notice; the legislature's power to define crimes
a criminal statute is still ambiguous after the ordinary tools are used
one fair reading raises serious constitutional doubts and another does not
a reading would alter the federal-state balance, abrogate state immunity, apply a law retroactively or outside the country
Congress's role in deciding major policy
an agency claims power of vast economic or political significance from vague words

blocks.html: The rule of lenity is old: in United States v. Wiltberger (1820) Chief Justice Marshall wrote that the power of punishment is vested in the legislature, not the courts, so courts should not stretch criminal laws to cover cases the words do not clearly reach. Avoidance assumes Congress means to act within the Constitution and lets courts avoid striking laws down. Clear-statement rules protect structural arrangements that Congress should not be presumed to disturb by accident. The major questions doctrine, rooted in FDA v. Brown & Williamson (2000), requires clear authorization when an agency claims power over a question of vast economic and political significance. Supporters say it keeps major policy choices with the elected Congress; critics say it is a judge-made limit not found in the text and can block agencies from using powers Congress gave in broad terms.

blocks.title: Lenity
blocks.q: A statute increases the sentence for anyone who "uses a weapon" during a robbery. Courts disagree whether showing a gun without firing it is "use." After text, context and history, the question is still evenly balanced. What does lenity suggest?
steps: Lenity applies only to real ambiguity that remains after the ordinary tools.
Here it remains.
Choose the narrower reading, favoring the defendant.
blocks.a: Read "uses" narrowly; the enhancement does not apply.

blocks.title: Avoidance
blocks.q: A statute lets officials refuse permits to groups that are "disruptive." Read broadly, it could punish unpopular speech, raising serious First Amendment doubts. Read narrowly, it covers only physical disruption of traffic. What does the avoidance canon suggest?
steps: Two fair readings exist.
The broad one raises serious constitutional doubts; the narrow one does not.
Adopt the narrow one, without deciding whether the broad one would be unconstitutional.
blocks.a: The narrow reading (physical disruption).

blocks.name: cv-sort

cards.text: An unclear criminal penalty is read narrowly.
A reading that would raise serious free-speech doubts is passed over.
A general law is not read to let states be sued unless it says so plainly.
A statute is not applied retroactively absent clear words.

blocks.cap: Match each move to its canon.

blocks.html: Applying lenity whenever a criminal statute is hard to read. Courts generally use it only when real ambiguity remains after the other tools of interpretation (text, structure, context and, for some judges, history). Check: have you tried the ordinary tools first? Lenity is a tie-breaker, not a starting point.
This is an educational course, not legal advice.

Federal agencies apply hundreds of statutes every day and must decide what they mean. When a court reviews an agency's action, whose reading of the statute counts? The Court has answered in different ways over eighty years. You saw the setting in holding the bureaucracy accountable. Like the substantive canons, deference rules tell a court which way to lean when a statute is unclear.

blocks.name: cv-timeline

events.label: Skidmore: weight by power to persuade

blocks.cap: Eighty years of judicial review of agency interpretations.

blocks.html: Under Skidmore (1944), an agency's reading gets weight according to its power to persuade: the thoroughness of its reasoning, its consistency and its expertise. Under Chevron (1984), courts deferred to an agency's reasonable reading of an ambiguous statute it administered. Mead (2001) limited Chevron to agency readings carrying the force of law. The Court overruled Chevron in 2024; courts now decide for themselves what a statute means, giving agency views the weight their reasoning earns, as under Skidmore.

head: Skidmore (1944)
Chevron (1984)
rows: the court decides, weighing the agency's view
the court accepts any reasonable agency reading (step two)
weight depends on care, consistency and expertise
agencies have experience and information courts lack
Congress was presumed to leave gaps for agencies to fill

blocks.html: Chevron rested on a presumption that when Congress left a gap or ambiguity in a statute an agency administers, it meant the agency, which has expertise and answers to an elected President, to fill it. Skidmore rested on a different idea: an agency's reading is evidence of the best meaning, and it persuades to the degree its reasoning is careful and consistent. In United States v. Mead Corp. (2001) the Court said Chevron applied only when Congress had given the agency power to make rules carrying the force of law and the agency used it, as in notice-and-comment rulemaking; other agency readings, such as tariff rulings, got Skidmore weight. Judges and scholars long debated Chevron. Supporters said it respected expertise and political accountability; critics said it let agencies, rather than courts, say what the law is.

blocks.name: cv-case

opts.facts: The Clean Air Act required permits for new or modified "stationary sources" of air pollution. The EPA let a whole plant count as one source (the "bubble" approach), so a company could add equipment without a permit if the plant's total emissions did not rise. An environmental group challenged the rule.
opts.reasoning: Justice Stevens: the statute did not say whether "source" meant a whole plant or each piece of equipment, and Congress had left the choice to the agency. The EPA's reading was reasonable, so the court should accept it.

blocks.cap: Chevron (1984), the case behind two-step deference.

blocks.title: Chevron's two steps
blocks.q: In 1995, an agency reads an unclear statutory term broadly. A court thinks the narrower reading is somewhat better, but the agency's is reasonable. What did the court do under Chevron?
steps: Step one: is the statute clear? No, it is ambiguous on this point.
Step two: is the agency's reading reasonable? Yes.
So the court defers, even though it would have chosen the narrower reading on its own.
blocks.a: It upheld the agency's reading.

blocks.title: Skidmore weight
blocks.q: An agency issues an informal guidance letter reading a statute. The letter is short, gives no reasons and contradicts the agency's own earlier letters. How much weight would it get under Skidmore?
steps: Skidmore weighs thoroughness, the validity of the reasoning and consistency with earlier and later statements.
No reasons and inconsistency weigh against it.
blocks.a: Little weight.

blocks.html: Mixing up Skidmore and Chevron. Under Skidmore the agency's reading persuades only as much as its reasoning earns; under Chevron a reasonable reading controlled. Another slip: describing Chevron as current law. The Court overruled it in 2024.
This is an educational course, not legal advice.

blocks.html: You have now seen the tools: text and ordinary meaning, purpose, legislative history, the canons and the courts' relation to agencies. Judges combine them into approaches, often called schools. This lesson puts the two main schools side by side, each as its best advocates would put it.

Textualism prizes fidelity to the enacted words, predictability and the legislature's role as lawmaker. Purposivism prizes making statutes work as intended. Most judges use text, structure, purpose, history and canons in some mix; the schools differ in which tools come first and which can override others.

head: Textualism, as its advocates put it
Purposivism, as its advocates put it
rows: the words that passed both houses and were signed
the words, understood as a reasonable means to the legislature's ends
text, plus purpose and (for many) legislative history
predictable; limits judges' discretion; respects the lawmaking process
statutes work as intended; avoids results no one wanted
purposes are vague and let judges pick results
wooden readings defeat the law's aims and make Congress's job impossible

blocks.html: Both schools claim to be faithful agents of the legislature. Textualists, led in recent decades by Justice Antonin Scalia, argue that the only thing Congress agrees on is the text, and that a statute's purposes are pursued only as far as its words go, because legislation is compromise. Purposivists answer that words have meaning only in light of what a speaker is trying to do, and that Congress writes quickly and generally, relying on courts to carry out its evident goals. Over the past few decades, textualist arguments have become more common in Supreme Court opinions, and judges who favor purpose now also start with careful attention to text. The debate continues about method, not about which outcomes are good.

blocks.title: Methods cross the usual lines
blocks.q: In Yates v. United States (2015), the fish case, which justices dissented, reading "tangible object" in its broad ordinary sense?
steps: The dissent was written by Justice Kagan.
It was joined by Justices Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas.
Justices often grouped differently on other issues joined a textualist reading, while the plurality used canons and context to read the words narrowly.
blocks.a: Justices Kagan, Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas.

blocks.title: Two good arguments
blocks.q: King v. Burwell (2015) asked whether tax credits under the Affordable Care Act were available on exchanges set up by the federal government, when the provision referred to an exchange "established by the State." State each side's main argument.
steps: Majority (6–3, Chief Justice Roberts): read in the context of the whole act and its design, the phrase covers federal exchanges too; otherwise the act's insurance markets would fail in many states, which Congress could not have meant.
Dissent (Justice Scalia): the words "established by the State" are plain, and a federal exchange is not established by a State; fixing the statute is Congress's job.
blocks.a: Majority: whole-act context and design; dissent: the plain words.

blocks.name: cv-sort

cards.text: Look at the ordinary meaning when the law was enacted.
Ask what problem Congress set out to solve.
Committee reports are useful evidence of meaning.
Statutes are compromises; go only as far as the words go.

blocks.cap: Which school leans on each argument?

blocks.html: Thinking one school always produces liberal or conservative results. Both schools have produced results surprising to their usual allies, and judges of every kind use both tools. The debate is about method. Check: describe the method a judge used without naming the outcome. That is what this course asks you to identify.
This is an educational course, not legal advice.

blocks.html: You know that a court needs jurisdiction over the kind of case and the parties. Federal courts face one more gate, written into Article III itself: they may decide only real disputes.

Article III extends the federal judicial power to "Cases" and "Controversies." So federal courts decide real disputes between adverse parties, with a concrete stake in the result, and they do not give advisory opinions. The doctrines that enforce this limit are called justiciability: standing, ripeness, mootness and the political question doctrine.

The limit keeps judges in their role. Courts decide questions best when two sides with something real at stake argue them on actual facts; abstract questions, answered in advance, would make judges into advisers or lawmakers. The tradition began early. In 1793 President Washington, through Secretary of State Jefferson, sent the justices a list of questions about treaties and neutrality in the European war. The justices declined to answer, pointing to the separation of powers and their role as a court of last resort. In Muskrat v. United States (1911) the Court refused to decide a suit Congress had arranged so the Court could test a law, because there was no real adversary. Federal courts may issue declaratory judgments (statements of the parties' rights) only when an actual controversy exists.

head: Doctrine
The question it asks
rows: Is this the right plaintiff: one personally injured?
Has the dispute become concrete, or is it too early?
Is there still a live dispute, or is it too late?
Is this a question for the political branches, not the courts?

blocks.title: A request for advice
blocks.q: A senator writes to the Supreme Court asking whether a bill she plans to introduce would be constitutional. What will the Court do?
steps: There is no case: no parties, no injury, no law yet.
Answering would be an advisory opinion, which Article III does not allow.
blocks.a: Decline. The question can be decided only if the law passes and someone with standing challenges it.

blocks.title: Some state courts differ
blocks.q: Massachusetts' governor asks the state's Supreme Judicial Court whether a proposed law would violate the state constitution. Can that court answer?
steps: Article III binds federal courts, not state courts.
The Massachusetts Constitution of 1780 lets the governor and legislature ask the justices for opinions on important questions of law.
Several other states allow advisory opinions too.
blocks.a: Yes. Its state constitution allows advisory opinions.

cards.text: A company fined under a regulation sues to overturn the fine
Two friends who agree on everything ask a court to rule on a law
The President asks the justices for legal advice
A landowner sues after the city seizes her land
A citizen asks the court to say a law would be unwise

blocks.name: cv-clause
blocks.cap: Article III, Section 2: the judicial power extends to "Cases" and "Controversies."

blocks.html: Thinking the Supreme Court can rule on any law it thinks unconstitutional. A court can rule only when a proper party brings a real case, and only on the questions that case presents. Many state courts can give advisory opinions, but federal courts cannot. Check: who is the plaintiff, what is the injury, and what would a ruling change for them?
This is an educational course, not legal advice.

blocks.html: The first justiciability question is about the plaintiff. Many people may care about a law or a government action. Only some may sue over it. The doctrine that sorts them is standing.

To have standing a plaintiff must show (1) an injury in fact that is concrete, particularized and actual or imminent; (2) causation: the injury is fairly traceable to the defendant's conduct; and (3) redressability: a favorable ruling is likely to fix it. (Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, 1992.)

blocks.name: cv-sort

cards.text: The factory's smoke blows onto my farm and kills my crops.
The smoke comes from this factory, not from a distant fire.
An order limiting the factory's emissions would protect my next crop.
I lost \$4,000 when the city refused my permit.
Ordering the city to reconsider could lead to the permit.

blocks.cap: Which element does each statement help prove?

blocks.html: Standing ties a lawsuit to a person with a personal stake, which keeps courts deciding concrete disputes rather than policy questions in the abstract. A harm shared equally by every citizen, such as an interest in the government obeying the law, is a generalized grievance; the remedy for it lies with voters and their representatives. So, as a rule, being a federal taxpayer does not by itself give standing to challenge how money is spent (the Court has recognized only a narrow exception for some religion-clause claims). The test has three parts because each closes a gap: the plaintiff must be hurt, by this defendant, in a way the court can help. In Spokeo, Inc. v. Robins (2016) the Court held that the injury must be concrete as well as particularized: a bare procedural violation of a statute, divorced from any real harm, is not enough.

blocks.title: Lujan
blocks.q: Members of wildlife groups said they had visited habitats of endangered species abroad and intended to return "someday." They challenged a rule that limited a federal consultation duty to actions in the United States. Did they have standing?
steps: Injury in fact must be actual or imminent.
"Someday" intentions, without concrete plans, are not imminent.
The Court (7–2 in the judgment) held they lacked standing.
blocks.a: No: no imminent injury in fact.

blocks.title: Which element fails?
blocks.q: A driver sues a car maker, alleging that the maker's ad campaign raised gas prices nationwide, so she pays more at the pump. Assume she does pay more. Which element is weakest?
steps: Injury: higher prices are concrete and personal. Present.
Causation: gas prices depend on many independent actors (producers, markets, sellers). Tracing her higher price to one company's ads is speculative.
Redressability falls with it: stopping the ads would not likely lower her price.
blocks.a: Causation (and so redressability).

blocks.name: cv-case
blocks.cap: Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife (1992), the source of the three-part test.

blocks.html: Thinking caring deeply about an issue gives standing. A general interest shared by all citizens is not enough, however sincere or strong; the plaintiff needs a personal, concrete injury. Check each element against the plaintiff's own situation: what happened to this person, caused by this defendant, fixable by this court?
This is an educational course, not legal advice.
A plaintiff with standing must also come to court at the right time. Too early, and the case is not ripe. Too late, and it is moot. Both doctrines keep courts deciding live, concrete disputes.

A case is not ripe if the harm is too speculative or the dispute not yet concrete. A case is moot if events end the dispute, unless an exception applies, such as a wrong "capable of repetition, yet evading review" or a defendant's voluntary stop that it could resume.

blocks.name: cv-timeline

events.label: A city proposes a parade rule (not ripe)
The rule is adopted; the group must change its plans (ripe)
The city repeals the rule for good (moot)

blocks.cap: An invented example. Ripeness asks "too early?"; mootness asks "too late?"

blocks.html:
Ripeness keeps courts from deciding disputes that may never happen or whose facts are not yet known. In Abbott Laboratories v. Gardner (1967) the Court framed a two-part inquiry: the fitness of the issues for decision (is it a purely legal question, or does it need more facts?) and the hardship to the parties of waiting (must they change their conduct now or risk penalties?). A person need not break a law and be prosecuted to challenge it if the threat of enforcement is real.

Mootness is standing over time: the personal stake must last through the whole case. If the dispute ends (the plaintiff graduates, the law is repealed, the parties settle), the court dismisses. Exceptions keep important questions reviewable: some wrongs are too short to finish litigating but likely to recur to the same person (capable of repetition, yet evading review); a defendant cannot moot a case just by stopping, unless it is absolutely clear the conduct could not reasonably be expected to recur (voluntary cessation, as in Friends of the Earth v. Laidlaw, 2000); and a criminal conviction with lasting collateral consequences can be challenged after the sentence ends.

blocks.title: Too early?
blocks.q: A state agency is considering a rule that might someday require labs to change their reporting forms. No rule has been proposed. A lab sues to block it. Ripe?
steps: Fitness: no rule text exists, so the court cannot know what it would require.
Hardship: the lab need not change anything now.
blocks.a: Not ripe.

blocks.title: Too late?
blocks.q: A student sues to stop his school from enforcing a dress-code rule against him. Before the appeal is decided, he graduates. Moot? Any exception?
steps: He no longer attends the school, so the rule can't affect him: the dispute has ended for him.
Capable of repetition? Not to him: he has graduated.
Voluntary cessation? The school did not stop; the student left.
blocks.a: Moot (unless the suit was a class action or he seeks damages for past harm).

blocks.name: cv-sort

cards.text: Suit over a law the legislature may pass next year
Suit over a contract after the parties settle
A company stops polluting the week it is sued, but could start again
Challenge to a fine the plaintiff must pay now
Challenge to a permit denial after the permit is granted

blocks.cap: Too early, too late, or just right?

blocks.html: Mixing up the two by timing. Ripeness asks "too early?" (has the dispute become concrete?); mootness asks "too late?" (is the dispute still alive?). Check: is the event that would create the injury still in the future (ripeness) or has the dispute already ended (mootness)?
This is an educational course, not legal advice.

blocks.html: The last justiciability doctrine concerns not the plaintiff or the timing but the question itself. Some questions, even when properly brought, are for the political branches to answer. They are political questions, and the doctrine is narrower than its name suggests. It builds on ripeness and mootness.

Courts decline questions that the Constitution commits to another branch or that lack judicially manageable standards. Baker v. Carr (1962) listed the factors. Examples include Senate impeachment trials (Nixon v. United States, 1993) and partisan gerrymandering claims in federal court (Rucho v. Common Cause, 2019).

items: a textually demonstrable commitment of the issue to another branch;
a lack of judicially discoverable and manageable standards for resolving it;
the impossibility of deciding without an initial policy determination of a kind for nonjudicial discretion;
the impossibility of deciding without expressing lack of the respect due the other branches;
an unusual need for unquestioning adherence to a political decision already made;
the potential for embarrassment from conflicting statements by different branches.

blocks.html: The doctrine follows from the separation of powers. Some decisions belong to Congress or the President by the Constitution's design, and some questions cannot be decided by legal rules at all. In Luther v. Borden (1849) the Court left to Congress and the President the question of which of two rival governments of Rhode Island was legitimate. But in Baker v. Carr (6–2), the Court held that a challenge to badly unequal state legislative districts under the Equal Protection Clause was justiciable, leading to "one person, one vote." In Powell v. McCormack (1969) it decided whether the House could exclude a member-elect who met the Constitution's qualifications. In Nixon v. United States, a federal judge removed by the Senate argued that letting a committee hear the evidence was not a proper "trial"; the Court held that the Constitution gives the Senate the "sole Power to try" impeachments. In Rucho (5–4), the majority held that no judicially manageable standard exists for deciding how much partisanship in districting is too much; the dissent argued that courts could apply standards like those used by lower courts.

blocks.name: cv-case

opts.facts: Walter Nixon, a federal district judge, was convicted of perjury and impeached. A Senate committee took evidence and reported to the full Senate, which convicted and removed him. He argued the full Senate had to hear the evidence.

blocks.cap: Not President Nixon: Judge Walter Nixon, removed in 1989.

blocks.title: Political question or not?
blocks.q: A citizen sues, claiming her state's legislative districts are so unequal in population that her vote counts a fifth as much as others'. Is this a political question?
steps: Baker v. Carr held such equal protection claims are justiciable.
Population equality is a manageable standard: count the people.
blocks.a: No. Courts decide malapportionment claims.

blocks.title: Another one
blocks.q: A voter sues in federal court, claiming her state's congressional map was drawn to favor one party too much. After Rucho, can a federal court decide the claim?
steps: Rucho held partisan gerrymandering claims present political questions beyond the reach of federal courts.
State courts, applying state constitutions or statutes, and Congress may still act.
blocks.a: No, not in federal court; state law and Congress remain possible routes.

blocks.html: Thinking any case about politics is a political question. Many politically charged cases are decided: elections, districting by population, the House's exclusion of a member, even a President's claims of privilege. The doctrine is narrow and turns on the Baker factors. Check: does the Constitution give this decision to another branch, or are there no legal standards to apply? If neither, the court will decide.
This is an educational course, not legal advice.

The last unit is a first look at four subjects that fill the first year of law school. Each uses the tools you have learned: elements, burdens of proof and case-by-case reasoning. We start with contracts, the law of enforceable promises, mostly state common law (and, for sales of goods, the Uniform Commercial Code).

A contract is a promise the law will enforce. It generally needs an offer, an acceptance and consideration (a bargained-for exchange). When a contract is broken, remedies usually aim to give the injured party the benefit of the bargain: what they would have had if the promise had been kept.

blocks.name: cv-order
blocks.cap: The life of a contract, in order.

blocks.html: Why enforce some promises and not others? The law enforces bargains: each side gives or promises something in exchange for what the other gives. That exchange (consideration) marks a promise as a deal rather than a gift or a social plan. In Hamer v. Sidway (New York, 1891), an uncle promised his nephew \$5,000 if the nephew gave up drinking, smoking, swearing and gambling until age 21. The nephew did. The court held that giving up a legal right was consideration, even if it benefited the nephew, so the promise was enforceable. Contracts can still fail for defenses such as lack of capacity (a minor), duress, fraud, some mistakes, illegality or unconscionability.

head: Remedy
Aim
rows: put the injured party where performance would have put them (the usual measure)
repay what the injured party spent relying on the promise
return a benefit the other party received
a court order to perform, used when money is not enough, as with a unique item or land

blocks.title: Is there a contract?
blocks.q: Kim says to Lee, "I'll sell you my bike for \$90." Lee says, "Deal." Later, Kim's friend offers \$120, and Kim tells Lee the deal is off. Is there a contract?
steps: Offer: Kim proposed definite terms (the bike, \$90).
Acceptance: Lee agreed to those exact terms.
Consideration: the bike in exchange for \$90, a bargain.
A sale of goods under \$500 need not be written (see below), so the oral deal can be enforced.
blocks.a: Yes. Kim is bound; if she sells to the friend, Lee can recover his lost bargain.

blocks.title: A gift promise
blocks.q: An aunt promises her niece \$1,000 for her birthday, asking nothing in return, and then changes her mind. Can the niece enforce the promise?
steps: Offer and acceptance in a loose sense, but no bargain: the niece gives nothing in exchange.
A promise to make a gift lacks consideration.
(Some courts enforce such promises if the niece reasonably relied on them to her detriment, a doctrine called promissory estoppel.)
blocks.a: Usually no: no consideration.

blocks.html: Thinking a contract must be written to be enforceable. Many oral contracts are enforceable. The statute of frauds (from an English statute of 1677) requires a signed writing only for certain kinds: sales of interests in land, contracts that cannot be performed within one year, promises to pay another person's debt, contracts in consideration of marriage, an executor's promise to pay estate debts personally, and (under the UCC) sales of goods for \$500 or more. Check: does the deal fall in one of those categories?
This is an educational course, not legal advice.

A tort is a civil wrong, other than a breach of contract, for which a court gives a remedy, usually money. Tort law is mostly state common law, built up case by case, and it is private law: the injured person sues (see public and private law).

A tort is a civil wrong. Negligence requires a duty, a breach of that duty, causation (actual and proximate) and damages. Intentional torts include battery, assault and trespass. Strict liability applies, without fault, to a few activities, such as abnormally dangerous ones.

head: Kind
Fault required
Examples
rows: intent to do the act (or knowledge its result is substantially certain)
battery (harmful or offensive contact), assault (causing a reasonable fear of imminent contact), false imprisonment, trespass to land
a driver who runs a red light; a store that ignores a spill
blasting; keeping wild animals; many claims for defective products

blocks.html: Tort law shifts the cost of an injury to the person responsible for it, which compensates the injured and gives everyone reason to take care. Negligence measures care against the reasonable person: what would a reasonably careful person have done? Causation has two parts. Actual cause asks whether the harm would have happened "but for" the conduct. Proximate cause limits liability to harms that were a foreseeable result of the risk. In Palsgraf v. Long Island Railroad Co. (New York, 1928, 4–3), railroad guards pushed a man onto a moving train; he dropped a package of fireworks, which exploded, and a scale some distance away fell on Helen Palsgraf. Chief Judge Benjamin Cardozo held the railroad owed her no duty, because no harm to her was foreseeable from the guards' conduct. Most states now use comparative negligence, reducing a plaintiff's award by her own share of fault.

blocks.name: cv-order
blocks.cap: The four elements of negligence, in the order courts usually analyze them.

blocks.title: Which element is missing?
blocks.q: A driver texting at a red light rolls forward and taps the bumper of the car ahead. There is no dent, no injury, and no cost of any kind. The other driver sues for negligence. Who wins?
steps: Duty: drivers owe others reasonable care. Yes.
Breach: texting and rolling forward is careless. Yes.
Causation: the tap was caused by the conduct. Yes.
Damages: none at all.
blocks.a: The texting driver: negligence requires actual damages.

blocks.title: Intent without touching
blocks.q: Ben swings a fist at Ana, who sees it coming and ducks; he misses. Battery, assault, both or neither?
steps: Battery requires a harmful or offensive contact: none happened.
Assault requires causing a reasonable apprehension of an imminent contact: Ana saw the swing coming.
blocks.a: Assault, not battery.

blocks.html: Thinking any accident means someone was negligent. Negligence needs a breach of the duty of reasonable care, plus causation and harm. Many accidents happen even when everyone acts reasonably, and then no one is liable in negligence. Check: what would a reasonable person have done differently?

blocks.html: Criminal law defines the conduct the government punishes. You have seen the path of a criminal case and the reasonable-doubt standard. Here is what the prosecution must prove: the elements of the crime.

Most crimes require a guilty act (actus reus) and a guilty mind (mens rea). The Model Penal Code ranks mental states as purposely, knowingly, recklessly and negligently. Defenses include justifications, such as self-defense, and excuses, such as insanity.

head: Mental state (Model Penal Code)
Meaning
Example
rows: it is your conscious object to cause the result
aiming at a window to break it
you are aware the result is practically certain
burning your own shed for the insurance money, aware that the neighbor's attached garage will almost certainly burn too
you consciously disregard a substantial and unjustifiable risk
firing a gun into the air in a city
you should have been aware of a substantial and unjustifiable risk, and failing to see it is a gross deviation from reasonable care
leaving a loaded gun where a small child can reach it, without realizing the danger

blocks.html: Punishment expresses blame, and we blame people for choices, not for bad luck. So criminal law usually requires both an act (thoughts alone are not crimes; the act must be voluntary, or an omission where the law imposed a duty to act) and a culpable mental state that matches the crime's definition. The American Law Institute published the Model Penal Code in 1962 to bring order to many inconsistent terms; many states adopted parts of it. Some minor and regulatory offenses, such as many traffic violations, impose strict liability with no mental state, but courts usually presume that serious crimes require one. Justifications say the act was right under the circumstances (self-defense: a reasonable belief that force is needed against an imminent unlawful attack, with force proportional to the threat). Excuses say the act was wrong but the person is not blameworthy (insanity: under the M'Naghten rule of 1843, the defendant, because of mental disease, did not know the nature of the act or that it was wrong).

blocks.title: Name the mental state
blocks.q: A driver races through a school zone at 60 mph, knowing children may be crossing but hoping no one is hurt. A child is injured. Which MPC mental state fits best?
steps: Not purposely: injuring a child was not the driver's goal.
Not knowingly: injury was not practically certain.
The driver was aware of a substantial, unjustifiable risk and ignored it.
blocks.a: Recklessly.

blocks.title: Motive and intent
blocks.q: Rae takes bread from a store without paying, intending to keep it, to feed her hungry children. Does her motive defeat the mental element of theft?
steps: Theft requires the intent to take and keep another's property. Rae had that intent.
Her motive (to feed her children) explains why, but it is not an element.
Motive may matter at sentencing or for a narrow defense such as necessity, which has strict limits.
blocks.a: No. She had the required intent; motive is separate.

blocks.name: cv-order
blocks.cap: Order the Model Penal Code mental states from most to least culpable.

blocks.html: Thinking motive is the same as intent. Intent is the mental state toward the act or result (did she mean to take the property?); motive is the reason behind it (why did she want it?) and is usually not an element. A good motive does not erase intent, and a bad motive does not supply it. Check: does the statute's definition mention the reason? Usually it does not.

Federal agencies publish tens of thousands of pages of rules and notices in the Federal Register each year, and they decide a great many cases. Administrative law governs how they do it. It brings together the sources of law, the separation of powers and judicial review of agency interpretations.

Agencies make rules, adjudicate cases and enforce laws under powers granted by statutes. The Administrative Procedure Act (1946) requires notice-and-comment rulemaking for most rules and lets courts set aside agency action that is "arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law."

blocks.name: cv-order

items: Congress passes a statute delegating authority
The agency publishes a proposed rule in the Federal Register
The agency publishes a final rule, answering significant comments
The rule takes effect and is codified in the Code of Federal Regulations
Courts review the rule if it is challenged

blocks.cap: Notice-and-comment rulemaking, in order.

blocks.html: Congress cannot write every technical detail, so it passes statutes that set goals and delegate authority to agencies. Under the nondelegation doctrine, Congress must give an "intelligible principle" to guide the agency (J.W. Hampton, Jr. & Co. v. United States, 1928). The APA, signed June 11, 1946, sets fair procedures. For most rules (called legislative rules) the agency must publish notice, take comments and explain the final rule, and such rules have the force of law. Interpretive rules and policy statements, which explain how the agency reads the law, are exempt from notice and comment and do not bind the public the same way. Agencies also decide cases, often before administrative law judges. All three branches check the process: courts review it under the APA, the President directs most agencies, and Congress funds them and can overturn rules by passing a new law, including under the Congressional Review Act (1996).

blocks.name: cv-branches
blocks.cap: Three checks that reach agencies: money, confirmation of their leaders and judicial review.

blocks.title: Arbitrary and capricious
blocks.q: An agency withdraws a safety rule. Its notice gives no reason and does not respond to evidence in the record that the rule saved lives. A group sues. What is the likely result?
steps: Under the APA a court sets aside action that is arbitrary and capricious.
Courts require an agency to examine the relevant data and give a reasoned explanation, including for changing course.
No reason and no response to the evidence fails that test.
blocks.a: The court will likely set the withdrawal aside and send it back to the agency.

blocks.title: Which kind of rule?
blocks.q: An agency posts a guidance document explaining how it reads an existing regulation. It took no public comments. Is the guidance invalid for skipping notice and comment?
steps: Notice and comment is required for legislative rules that bind the public.
Interpretive guidance is exempt.
But because it skipped the process, it does not carry the force of law the way a legislative rule does.
blocks.a: No, it is not invalid, but it does not bind the public like a legislative rule.

blocks.html: Thinking agency rules are only guidance. Legislative rules made through proper procedures under a valid statute have the force of law: violating them can bring fines or other penalties. Check: was the rule issued through notice and comment under authority a statute grants? If so, it binds like a statute.
